- signs of dehydration or a salt imbalance, such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, confusion, muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat or unusual weakness
Other side effects:
Other hydrochlorothiazide side effects include:
- dizziness, a spinning sensation (vertigo), headache, restlessness, or tingling and numbness (paresthesia)
- weakness
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, stomach cramping, stomach irritation, or loss of appetite
- muscle spasm
- increased sensitivity to sunlight, causing sunburn more easily
- hair loss or thinning
- difficulty getting or keeping an erection
- temporary blurred vision, or objects looking yellow-tinged (xanthopsia)
- swelling and tenderness of the salivary glands
- raised blood sugar, sugar in the urine, or raised uric acid

If a side effect is moderate or severe, your doctor may lower your dose or stop the medicine. Do not stop taking HCTZ on your own without speaking to your doctor first.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Fluid and salt imbalance:
Hydrochlorothiazide can lower the levels of potassium, sodium, magnesium and chloride in your blood. Low potassium (hypokalemia) is the most common of these and is more likely at higher doses, during rapid fluid loss, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after long-term use.. Your doctor will check your blood before you start and at intervals during treatment.
Contact your doctor if you have any of the following, which can be signs of a fluid or salt imbalance:
- dry mouth, thirst, or unusual weakness or tiredness
- drowsiness, restlessness or confusion
- muscle pain, cramps or muscle fatigue
- fast heartbeat
- passing much less urine than usual
- nausea or vomiting
- seizures
Kidney and liver problems:

HCTZ reduces the fluid volume in your body, which can lead to sudden kidney injury. The risk is higher if you have chronic kidney disease, heart failure, or are already low on fluid. If you have liver disease, small changes in fluid and salt balance can trigger a serious complication called hepatic coma. Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and watch for changes in alertness.
Sudden vision changes need urgent care:
Rarely, hydrochlorothiazide causes sudden short-sightedness (acute myopia) and a sharp rise in pressure inside the eye (acute angle-closure glaucoma), usually within hours to weeks of starting the medicine. Stop taking it and get medical help immediately if your vision drops suddenly or your eye hurts. Left untreated, this can cause permanent loss of vision. A history of allergy to sulfa medicines or penicillin may increase the risk.
Blood sugar, cholesterol, uric acid and calcium:

Hydrochlorothiazide can raise blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides, uric acid and calcium. Your diabetes medicine or insulin dose may need adjusting, and diabetes that was previously unnoticed can become apparent during treatment. The rise in uric acid is related to the dose and can cause gout or make existing gout worse. Because the medicine also affects calcium, it is stopped before parathyroid function tests, so tell any doctor arranging tests that you take it. Your doctor will check these levels from time to time.
Skin cancer risk:
Long-term use of hydrochlorothiazide is linked to a small increase in the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, mainly squamous cell carcinoma. In a large safety study the increase was about 1 extra case per 16,000 people per year, rising to about 1 extra case per 6,700 people per year among white patients who had taken a total of 50,000 mg or more.

Protect your skin from the sun, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen, avoid sunlamps and tanning beds, and have regular skin checks. Tell your doctor about any new or changing skin growth, or a sore that does not heal.
Lupus and allergic reactions:
Thiazide diuretics have been reported to worsen lupus or bring it on. Sensitivity reactions can happen whether or not you have a history of allergies or asthma.

Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic, often called a water pill, used to treat high blood pressure and to reduce a build-up of fluid in the body (edema). It works by making the kidneys pass more salt and water out of the body, so you urinate more.
Hydrochlorothiazide is often shortened to HCTZ on prescriptions and medical records. It is available as a tablet, capsule, and liquid (suspension) taken by mouth and is usually taken once or twice a day.
Hydrochlorothiazide is available as:
- oral tablet (12.5 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg)
- oral capsule (12.5 mg)
- powder for oral suspension (10 mg/mL)
Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) brand names included HydroDIURIL tablets (discontinued), Esidrix (discontinued), and Microzide capsules (discontinued); now generic tablets and capsules are available. The brand name of hydrochlorothiazide oral suspension is Inzirqo.
Hydrochlorothiazide is also an ingredient in many combination blood pressure medicines, including with losartan, lisinopril, valsartan, and more.

Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients.
High blood pressure:
HCTZ is used to manage high blood pressure (hypertension), either on its own or alongside other blood pressure medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, mainly strokes and heart attacks.
All three forms of hydrochlorothiazide, tablets, capsules and the oral suspension, are approved for high blood pressure in adults, and the oral suspension is also approved for children.
Fluid retention:
Hydrochlorothiazide tablets are used to treat a build-up of fluid (edema) associated with:
- congestive heart failure
- cirrhosis of the liver
- kidney conditions, including nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney failure
- treatment with corticosteroid or estrogen medicines
The HCTZ oral suspension is approved for fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and kidney disease including nephrotic syndrome, in both adults and children.

The capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
Not all forms of HCTZ are approved for all indications and age groups.
Approved HCTZ uses by age groups and dosage form:
HCTZ Form and strengths | High blood pressure | Fluid retention (edema) | Ages
Tablets 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg | Yes | As an add-on therapy for edema due to congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and corticosteroid and estrogen therapy. Yes, for edema due to various forms of renal dysfunction such as nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis, and chronic renal failure. | Adults and children
Capsules 12.5 mg | Yes | No | Adults
Oral suspension 10 mg/mL | Yes | Yes, for edema due to congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and renal disease including the nephrotic syndrome in adult and pediatric patients. | Adults and children

Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
- Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
- Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. The doses need to be separated. For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin.
- NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin. These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended.

- Insulin and oral diabetes medicines. Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting.
- Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.
- Digoxin and other digitalis medicines. Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms.
- Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.
- Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.
- Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine). You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide.
- Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine). Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use.
This list is not complete. Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.

Do not take hydrocodone and acetaminophen if you have:
- Severe asthma, trouble breathing, or other lung problems
- A bowel blockage or a narrowing of the stomach or intestines
- Signs of an allergy, such as a rash
- Are allergic to any of its ingredients.
Before taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of:
- Head injury, seizures
- Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
- Problems urinating
- Pancreas or gallbladder problems
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
- Pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Prolonged use of hydrocodone and acetaminophen during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated
- Breastfeeding. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen pass into breast milk and may harm your baby. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

- Taking prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. Taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen with certain other medicines can cause serious side effects that could lead to death.

Adult Dose of Hydrocodone And Acetaminophen for Moderate to Severe Pain:
Hydrocodone 2.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet, Hydrocodone 5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 to 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 8 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg, Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet:
- Initial dose: 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 6 tablets/24 hours
Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 15 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours
Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 300 mg per 15 mL oral solution:
- Initial dose: 11.25 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
- Maximum dose: 67.5 mL/24 hours
Comments:
- Doses should be individually titrated to provide adequate analgesia while minimizing adverse reactions.
- Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse, the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with individual patient treatment goals should be used.
- Monitor patients closely for respiratory depression within the first 24 to 72 hours of initiating therapy and following any increase in dose.

When taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen:
- Do not change your dose. Take hydrocodone and acetaminophen exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
- Take your prescribed dose every four to six hours at the same time every day. Do not take more than your prescribed dose. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- If taking the oral solution, always use a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup to correctly measure your dose. Never use a household teaspoon or tablespoon to measure your medicine.
- Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain, if your pain gets worse, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain. Do not take more medicine without first talking to your healthcare provider.
If you have been taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen regularly, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider.
After you stop taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, flush any unused tablets or oral solution down the toilet.

Get emergency help right away if you take too many hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets or oral solution (overdose). When you first start taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur.
Never give anyone else your hydrocodone and acetaminophen. They could die from taking them. Store hydrocodone and acetaminophen away from children and in a safe place to prevent stealing or abuse. Selling or giving away hydrocodone and acetaminophen products is against the law.

Common Side Effects:
The possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen are constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and abdominal pain. Call your healthcare provider if you have any of these symptoms and they are severe.
Get emergency medical help if you have:
- Trouble breathing
- Shortness of breath
- Fast heartbeat
- Chest pain
- Swelling of your face, tongue, or throat
- Extreme drowsiness
- Light-headedness when changing positions
- Feeling faint
- Agitation
- High body temperature
- Trouble walking
- Stiff muscles
- Mental changes such as confusion.
These are not all the possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.

Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department. Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it.
The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness. Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a strong prescription combination pain medicine containing an opioid, hydrocodone, in addition to acetaminophen, which is used to manage moderate to moderately severe pain, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
An opioid pain medicine that can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a Schedule II controlled substance.
All branded hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, Hycet, Lorcet, Verdrocet, Xodol, Zamicet) have been discontinued, but generic hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets and oral solution is still available.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen first gained FDA approval on May 3, 1982.

This list is not complete. Other drugs may interact with acetaminophen and hydrocodone, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. To check for interactions with hydrocodone and acetaminophen, click the link below.
Remember, keep this and all other medicines out of the reach of children, never share your medicines with others, and use acetaminophen or hydrocodone only for the indication prescribed.

While taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, DO NOT:
- Drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how hydrocodone and acetaminophen affects you. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen can make you sleepy, dizzy, or lightheaded.
- Drink alcohol or use prescription or over-the-counter medicines that contain alcohol. Using products containing alcohol during treatment with hydrocodone and acetaminophen may cause you to overdose and die.
No. Alcohol's effects may be stronger while you are taking hydroxyzine. You should also avoid other medicines that slow down the central nervous system.

Weight gain is not among the side effects reported in FDA-approved labeling for hydroxyzine. It does not appear in the labeling for the tablets, the oral solution, the pamoate capsules, or the injection.
This does not mean weight changes are impossible for every person. If your weight changes while you are taking hydroxyzine, tell your doctor.

Take hydroxyzine exactly as your doctor prescribes. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Do not take more or less than prescribed, and do not take it for longer than your doctor tells you to.
Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how well you respond to treatment.
If you are taking the oral solution, measure your dose with the dosing syringe provided, a dose-measuring spoon, or a medicine cup. Do not use a kitchen spoon, because it will not give an accurate dose. Ask your pharmacist for a measuring device if you do not have one.
Call your doctor if your anxiety does not improve or if it gets worse.

Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain, below the outer layer known as the cortex. It is not a cortical depressant, meaning it does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain the way some other sedatives do.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle, widens the airways (bronchodilation), and reduces pain. These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.
Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting. This is an approved use for the injection, but not for the forms taken by mouth.
Hydroxyzine usually starts working within 15 to 30 minutes of taking it by mouth. It is absorbed quickly from the digestive system. This is the same for tablets, oral solution, and pamoate capsules.

Store hydroxyzine tablets, capsules, and oral solution at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C).
Keep tablets and capsules in a tightly closed, light-resistant container with a child-resistant cap.
Keep the oral solution in a tightly closed, light-resistant bottle with a child-resistant cap. Protect it from light and do not let it freeze.
Keep this and all medicines out of the reach of children.

The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.

In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.

If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
The most common sign of hydroxyzine overdose is heavy sedation. Other reported signs include seizures (convulsions), stupor, nausea, and vomiting.
Overdose can also cause QT prolongation and Torsade de Pointes, so heart monitoring with an ECG is recommended.
There is no specific antidote for hydroxyzine overdose.

Hydroxyzine is a prescription antihistamine used to treat anxiety and tension, itching from allergic skin conditions, and sedation before and after general anesthesia.
It comes in three oral forms:
- Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths
- Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL
- Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg
There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection. It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin.
Hydroxyzine is not chemically related to benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, reserpine, or meprobamate.

Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses. These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
- Anxiety and tension. For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
- Itching from allergic skin conditions. For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant. It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
- Sedation around surgery. As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings. It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety. Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months. Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine. Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses, the same doses, the same warnings, and the same side effects.
The injection is the exception. It is a hydroxyzine HCl product; there is no pamoate injection, and it has its own approved uses, doses, and warnings.
The practical differences are:
- Form. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution. Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.
- How they dissolve. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride is very soluble in water. Hydroxyzine pamoate is practically insoluble in water.
- How the strength is measured. Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by the amount of hydroxyzine HCl they are equivalent to. A 25 mg pamoate capsule delivers the same amount of active medicine as a hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg tablet.

The two salts also had different brand names. Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate, and Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride. Both brands have been discontinued in the United States, and hydroxyzine is now available as a generic medicine.
Is hydroxyzine pamoate stronger or longer lasting than hydroxyzine hydrochloride?:
No. You may read that hydroxyzine pamoate works better for anxiety, lasts longer, or reaches the brain more effectively than hydroxyzine hydrochloride. FDA-approved labeling does not support this.
Labeling for both salt forms states that hydroxyzine's effects are usually noticed within 15 to 30 minutes of a dose taken by mouth. Both are approved for the same three uses. Both carry the same doses, which are 50 to 100 mg four times a day for anxiety in adults, and 25 mg three or four times a day for itching. No FDA labeling describes a difference in how strongly or how long either form works.

The reason the doses match is that hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by their hydroxyzine hydrochloride equivalent. A 25 mg pamoate capsule and a 25 mg hydrochloride tablet deliver the same amount of active medicine.
If you feel that one form suits you better than the other, tell your doctor. People can respond differently to the same medicine.

The dose depends on what you are being treated for. The same doses apply to hydroxyzine hydrochloride tablets, hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution, and hydroxyzine pamoate capsules.
Dosage for anxiety and tension:
- Adults: 50 to 100 mg four times a day
- Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
- Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for itching:
- Adults: 25 mg three or four times a day
- Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
- Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for sedation before and after surgery:
- Adults: 50 to 100 mg
- Children: 0.6 mg for each kilogram of body weight
If treatment is started with an injection into a muscle, later doses can be given by mouth.
Dosage in older adults:

Doctors usually start older adults on a low dose. Sedating medicines can cause confusion and too much sedation in older people, so your doctor will watch you closely. Kidney, liver, and heart function often decline with age, and how much hydroxyzine leaves the body through the kidneys has not been established.

Hydroxyzine makes the effects of central nervous system depressants stronger. If you take hydroxyzine with any of the following, your doctor may need to lower the dose of the other medicine:
- narcotic (opioid) pain medicines
- non-narcotic pain medicines
- barbiturates
Hydroxyzine may increase the effects of meperidine and barbiturates when used before anesthesia, so your doctor will adjust these doses for you individually.
Care is needed if you take other medicines that can affect heart rhythm by prolonging the QT interval. These include:
- heart rhythm medicines such as quinidine, procainamide, amiodarone, and sotalol
- certain antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, and chlorpromazine
- certain antidepressants such as citalopram and fluoxetine
- certain antibiotics such as azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, and moxifloxacin
- other medicines such as pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, and droperidol

Hydroxyzine does not affect atropine or other belladonna alkaloids, and it is not known to interfere with digitalis. It can be used at the same time as digitalis.
Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here.

Hydroxyzine can make you drowsy. Do not drive or operate dangerous machinery until you know how it affects you.
Avoid alcohol and other medicines that cause drowsiness.

Tell your doctor if you have anything that raises your risk of a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation. This includes:
- congenital long QT syndrome, a heart rhythm condition you are born with
- a family history of long QT syndrome
- a recent heart attack
- heart failure that is not well controlled
- a slow or irregular heartbeat (bradyarrhythmia)
- other conditions that make heart rhythm problems more likely
Hydroxyzine should not be given to women who are breastfeeding. It is not known whether hydroxyzine passes into breast milk, but many medicines do.
The oral solution contains a small amount of alcohol, 0.5% by volume, and is sweetened with sucrose. Tell your doctor if either of these matters for you.

Do not take hydroxyzine if you:
- are allergic to hydroxyzine or to any ingredient in the medicine
- are allergic to cetirizine or levocetirizine
- have a prolonged QT interval, a heart rhythm finding seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG)
- are in early pregnancy
In animal studies, hydroxyzine caused birth defects in rats and mice at doses well above those used in people. There is not enough information in humans to know whether hydroxyzine is safe in early pregnancy, so it should not be used at that time.

Use ibuprofen exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor. Use the lowest dose that is effective in treating your condition.
An ibuprofen overdose can damage your stomach or intestines. The maximum amount of ibuprofen for adults is 800 milligrams per dose or 3200 mg per day (4 maximum doses).
A child's dose is based on the age and weight of the child. Carefully follow the dosing instructions provided with children's ibuprofen for the age and weight of your child. Ask a doctor or pharmacist if you have questions.
Take ibuprofen with food or milk to lessen stomach upset.
Shake the oral suspension (liquid) before you measure a dose. Use the dosing syringe provided, or use a medicine dose-measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
You must chew the chewable tablet before you swallow it.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat. Do not allow the liquid medicine to freeze.

- low red blood cells (anemia) - pale skin, feeling light-headed or short of breath, rapid heart rate, trouble concentrating; or
- kidney problems - little or no urinating, painful or difficult urination, swelling in your feet or ankles, feeling tired or short of breath.
Common ibuprofen side effects may include:
- nausea, vomiting, gas;
- bleeding; or
- dizziness, headache.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Ibuprofen can increase your risk of fatal heart attack, heart failure, or stroke. Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG). Avoid taking ibuprofen after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.
Ibuprofen may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal. These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Do not take more than your recommended dose. An ibuprofen overdose can damage your stomach or intestines. Use only the smallest amount of medication needed to get relief from your pain, swelling, or fever.
Since ibuprofen is used when needed, you may not be on a dosing schedule. Skip any missed dose if it's almost time for your next dose. Do not use two doses at one time.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. Overdose symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, drowsiness, black or bloody stools, coughing up blood, shallow breathing, fainting, or coma.

Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). It works by reducing hormones that cause inflammation and pain in the body.
Ibuprofen is used to reduce fever and treat pain or inflammation caused by many conditions such as headache, toothache, back pain, arthritis, menstrual cramps, or minor injury.
Ibuprofen is used in adults and children. Some formulations are also used in premature babies to close a certain heart defect.

Ask a doctor or pharmacist before using other medicines for pain, fever, swelling, or cold/flu symptoms. They may contain ingredients similar to ibuprofen (such as aspirin, ketoprofen, or naproxen).
Avoid taking aspirin unless your doctor tells you to.
If you also take aspirin to prevent stroke or heart attack, taking ibuprofen can make aspirin less effective in protecting your heart and blood vessels. If you take both medicines, take ibuprofen at least 8 hours before or 30 minutes after you take aspirin (non-enteric coated form).
Avoid drinking alcohol. It may increase your risk of stomach bleeding.

You should not use insulin glargine if you are allergic to insulin, or if you are having an episode of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) or diabetic ketoacidosis (call your doctor for treatment).
Different brands of insulin glargine are specifically approved for different age groups and different diabetes types. The safety and effectiveness of insulin glargine in pediatric patients younger than 6 years of age with type 1 diabetes and pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes has not been established.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- liver or kidney disease; or
- heart failure or other heart problems.
Tell your doctor if you also take pioglitazone or rosiglitazone (sometimes contained in combinations with glimepiride or metformin). Taking certain oral diabetes medicines while you are using insulin may increase your risk of serious heart problems.
Pregnancy:

Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant, as it is not known if insulin glargine will harm your unborn baby. Follow your doctor's instructions about using this medicine if you are pregnant or you become pregnant. Controlling diabetes is very important during pregnancy.
Breastfeeding:
Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or are planning to breastfeed, as it is not known if insulin glargine may harm your breastfeeding baby.

Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Use the medicine exactly as directed. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you don't understand how to use an injection.
Prepare an injection only when you are ready to give it. Do not use it if the medicine looks cloudy, has changed colors, or has particles in it.
Insulin glargine is injected under the skin, using a syringe or insulin pen, once per day at the same time of day.
Insulin can be injected into your upper legs (thighs), upper arms, or stomach area (abdomen). Do not inject into the same place two times in a row. Avoid injecting into skin that is damaged, tender, bruised, pitted, thickened, scaly, or has a scar or hard lump.
When treating type 1 diabetes, use your short-acting insulin before meals as directed by your doctor.
Insulin glargine must not be given with an insulin pump or mixed with other insulins. Do not inject insulin glargine into a vein or a muscle.

Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
If you use an injection pen, use only the injection pen that comes with insulin glargine. Attach a new needle before each use. Do not transfer the insulin from the pen into a syringe.
Never share an injection pen, even if you changed the needle. Sharing these devices can pass infections from person to person.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injections in case of severe hypoglycemia.
Tell your doctor if you have frequent symptoms of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia), such as increased thirst or urination. Ask your doctor before changing your medication dosage.

Wear a medical alert tag or carry an ID card to let others know you have diabetes.

Common insulin glargine side effects may include low blood sugar, swelling, weight gain, allergic reaction, itching, rash, or thickening or hollowing of the skin where you injected the medicine (lipodystrophy).
Serious insulin glargine side effects
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of insulin allergy: redness or swelling where an injection was given, itchy skin rash over the entire body, trouble breathing, fast heartbeats, feeling like you might pass out, or swelling in your tongue or throat.
Insulin glargine may cause other serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- rapid weight gain, swelling in your feet or ankles;
- shortness of breath; or
- low blood potassium--leg cramps, constipation, irregular heartbeats, fluttering in your chest, increased thirst or urination, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness or limp feeling.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Storing unopened (not in use) insulin glargine:
- Refrigerate at 36°F–46°F (2°C–8°C)
- Do NOT use after the expiration date.
Storing opened (in use) insulin glargine:
- Storage once in use varies for different brands of insulin glargine. For storage information for the different brands of insulin glargine while in use, check the prescribing information.
General storage information
- Keep this medicine in its original container protected from heat and light.
- Do not store an injection pen with the needle attached. Do not reuse a needle or syringe. Place them in a puncture-proof "sharps" container and dispose of it following state or local laws. Keep out of the reach of children and pets.
Never share an injection pen, even if you changed the needle.

Call your doctor for instructions if you miss a dose. Do not use more than one dose in a 24-hour period unless your doctor tells you to.
Get your prescription refilled before you run out of medicine completely.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. Insulin overdose can cause severe hypoglycemia. Symptoms include drowsiness, confusion, blurred vision, numbness or tingling in your mouth, trouble speaking, muscle weakness, clumsy or jerky movements, seizure (convulsions), or loss of consciousness.

Insulin glargine is a long-acting insulin used to treat type 1 and type 2 diabetes in certain patients to improve and maintain blood glucose levels. Insulin glargine is a man-made form of human insulin that is used once daily to provide a base level of insulin that keeps working for 24 hours or longer.
Insulin glargine is available under the brand names Lantus, Basaglar, Toujeo, Semglee, and Rezvoglar. Langlara is an interchangeable biosimilar to Lantus that was FDA-approved on May 4, 2026.
Rezvoglar, Lantus, Langlara, Semglee, and Toujeo are FDA-approved to be used for use in adult and pediatric patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Basasglar is FDA-approved to be used by adults for type 2 diabetes and also for adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes. In patients with type 1 diabetes, insulin glargine must be used together with a short-acting insulin.

Many drugs can affect your blood sugar and may also affect insulin glargine. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you use. Not all possible interactions are listed here.
Tell your doctor if you also take pioglitazone or rosiglitazone (sometimes contained in combinations with glimepiride or metformin). Taking certain oral diabetes medicines while you are using insulin may increase your risk of serious heart problems.

Avoid driving or hazardous activity until you know how insulin glargine will affect you. Your reactions could be impaired.
Avoid medication errors by always checking the medicine label before injecting your insulin.
Avoid drinking alcohol or using medicines that contain alcohol. It may interfere with your diabetes treatment.

Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Having hypothyroidism during pregnancy may increase the risk of miscarriage, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, or premature birth, and untreated hypothyroidism can affect the baby's brain development. The benefit of treating hypothyroidism outweighs these risks, and levothyroxine should not be stopped during pregnancy.
Your dose needs are often higher during pregnancy. Your doctor will check your thyroid blood tests as soon as your pregnancy is confirmed and at least once in each trimester, and will usually put you back on your pre-pregnancy dose straight after you give birth, with another blood test 4 to 8 weeks later.
Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Levothyroxine passes into breast milk, but no harmful effects on breastfed babies have been reported. Treating hypothyroidism properly may also help milk supply if it is low. Your dose needs may be different while you are nursing.
You may be more likely to have a broken bone while using levothyroxine, particularly if your dose is higher than you need. Talk with your doctor about ways to keep your bones healthy.

Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Some brands of levothyroxine have different dosage instructions and/or recommendations of how soon you need to take them before eating food. Always check the instructions on the label.
Oral levothyroxine:
Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution.
- Keep using this medicine even if you feel well. It may take 4 to 6 weeks to get the full benefit of a dose.
- You will need frequent medical tests, and your next dose may be delayed based on the results.
- This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
- Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery or dental procedure.
- Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Tablets and capsules:

Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water. A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly. Take the medicine at the same time each day.
- Swallow the capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it. Tell your doctor if your child cannot swallow a capsule whole.
- If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, crush the tablet and mix it with 1 or 2 teaspoons of water; give the mixture right away by spoon or dropper and make sure all of it is taken. Do not save it for later use. Do not mix it into soy-based infant formula or other foods that can stop levothyroxine being absorbed.
- Keep each tablet or capsule in the blister pack until you are ready to take one.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Oral solution (liquid medicine):
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).

- Dosages are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
- Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of levothyroxine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
- Tirosint-Sol oral solution comes in single-dose ampules and can be administered 15 minutes before eating breakfast. Squeeze the liquid directly into your mouth, onto a spoon, or into a glass of water to drink right away. Use all ampules within 3 months after opening the foil pouch.
- Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Store them in their original bottle. Use Ermeza within 90 days and Thyquidity within 8 weeks of opening the bottle.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Intravenous levothyroxine:
This is given as an injection into a vein by a healthcare provider and should only be used to treat myxedema coma.
Blood tests, biotin, and monitoring:

Your doctor will use blood tests to check that your dose is right, usually 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, and then every 6 to 12 months once your dose is stable. Children are tested more often, including 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment and 2 weeks after any dose change.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take biotin, or a multivitamin, hair, skin, or nail supplement that contains biotin (sometimes listed as vitamin B7). Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests and give a falsely high or falsely low result, which could lead to the wrong dose change. Stop biotin and any biotin-containing supplements at least 2 days before a thyroid blood test.
If your symptoms and blood tests still suggest an underactive thyroid even though you are on a dose that should be enough, it may be because the medicine is not being absorbed properly, doses are being missed, or another medicine is interfering. Talk to your doctor before your dose is increased.

Too much levothyroxine in babies can cause the soft spots on the skull to close too early, and in older children it can cause the growth plates to close too early, which may reduce final adult height. Too little levothyroxine can affect a child's learning and growth. This is why children need regular blood tests and check-ups.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Levothyroxine should not be used to treat obesity or weight problems. Dangerous side effects or death can occur from the misuse of this medicine, especially if you are taking any other weight-loss medications or appetite suppressants.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small. Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development. Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust it gradually based on blood tests.
You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions. Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack.

If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine. Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis.
Older adults and people with heart disease are usually started on a lower dose, because too much thyroid hormone can cause an irregular heartbeat (most commonly atrial fibrillation), angina, or other heart problems. Tell your doctor if you develop chest pain, breathlessness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures. This is more likely after menopause. Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels.
Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma. Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.

In a medical setting, you are not likely to miss a dose of levothyroxine injection.
Take the missed oral levothyroxine dose as soon as you remember, and then go back to your regular schedule. Do not use two doses at one time.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose can be fatal.
Overdose symptoms may include headache, leg cramps, tremors, feeling nervous or irritable, confusion, chest pain, shortness of breath, fast or pounding heartbeats, stroke, seizures, shock, and coma. Symptoms may not appear straight away and can take several days to develop, so get medical advice even if the person seems well.

Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.

Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

This list is not complete, and many other drugs may interact with levothyroxine. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible drug interactions are listed here.

Avoid the following food products within 1 hour of taking oral levothyroxine or the medication will not be as effective: grapefruit juice, infant soy formula, soybean flour, cottonseed meal, walnuts, and high-fiber foods. Grapefruit juice can both delay absorption and reduce the amount of levothyroxine that gets into your body.
If you eat or drink any of these regularly, tell your doctor, as your dose may need adjusting.

Take lisinopril exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose..

If you have high blood pressure, keep using lisinopril even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
Store tightly closed at room temperature, away from moisture and heat. Do not freeze.

Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems. In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure. These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.

Avoid getting up too fast from a sitting or lying position, or you may feel dizzy.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes, unless your doctor has told you to.
Avoid becoming overheated or dehydrated during exercise, in hot weather, or by not drinking enough fluids. Follow your doctor's instructions about the type and amount of liquids you should drink. In some cases, drinking too much liquid can be as unsafe as not drinking enough.

Losartan is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children at least 6 years old.
Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).
Losartan may not decrease the risk of stroke in African Americans who have these conditions.
Losartan is also used to treat kidney disease in people who have type 2 diabetes (condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood) and high blood pressure.
Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin II receptor antagonists. It works by blocking the action of certain natural substances that tighten the blood vessels, allowing the blood to flow more smoothly and the heart to pump more efficiently.

Sometimes it is not safe to use certain medicines at the same time. Some drugs can affect your blood levels of other drugs you use, which may increase side effects or make the medicines less effective.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines, especially:

Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke, especially if you use it long term or take high doses, or if you have heart disease. Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.

Meloxicam is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). It works by reducing hormones that cause pain, fever, and inflammation in the body.
Meloxicam is used to relieve pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness caused by osteoarthritis (arthritis caused by a breakdown of the lining of the joints) and rheumatoid arthritis (arthritis caused by swelling of the lining of the joints).
Meloxicam is also used to relieve the pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness caused by juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (a type of arthritis that affects children) in children 2 years of age and older.
IV meloxicam (brands Anjeso [discontinued], Qamzova, Xifyrm) is used for moderate to severe pain in adults, alone or in combination with non-NSAID analgesics.

Drinking alcohol may increase your risk of stomach bleeding.
Avoid taking aspirin while you are taking meloxicam, unless your doctor tells you to.
Ask a doctor or pharmacist before using other medicines for pain, fever, swelling, or cold/flu symptoms. They may contain ingredients similar to meloxicam (such as aspirin, ibuprofen, ketoprofen, or naproxen).

If you need to have surgery or any type of x-ray or CT scan using a dye that is injected into your veins, you may need to temporarily stop taking metformin. Be sure your caregivers know ahead of time that you are using this medication.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- kidney disease (your kidney function may need to be checked before you take this medicine);
- high ketone levels in your blood or urine;
- heart disease, congestive heart failure;
- liver disease or liver impairment
- if you also use insulin, or other oral diabetes medications.
You may develop lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood. This may be more likely if you have other medical conditions, a severe infection, chronic alcoholism, or if you are 65 or older. Ask your doctor about your risk.
Metformin immediate release tablets should not be given to a child younger than 10 years old.
This medicine should not be used for type 1 diabetes.
Pregnancy:

Follow your doctor's instructions about using metformin if you are pregnant or you become pregnant. Controlling diabetes is very important during pregnancy, and having high blood sugar may cause complications in both the mother and the baby. Tell your doctor if you become pregnant while taking metformin.
Metformin may stimulate ovulation in some women and may increase the risk of unintended pregnancy. Talk to your doctor about your risk.
Breastfeeding:
Talk to your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. Metformin can pass into your breast milk. Your healthcare provider will be able to advise you about the best way to feed your baby while you take this medicine.

You should not use metformin if you have:
- severe kidney disease, or
- metabolic acidosis or diabetic ketoacidosis (call your doctor for treatment), or
- an allergy to metformin or any of the inactive ingredients in this medicine.

Metformin is prescribed to manage polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) because it improves how the body responds to insulin. PCOS affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age and is often marked by insulin resistance, in which the body doesn't respond well to insulin, prompting the pancreas to produce more. This excess insulin drives up androgen (male hormone) production, worsening symptoms like irregular periods, infertility, acne, and excess hair growth. Metformin helps by lowering insulin levels, decreasing the liver's glucose production, improving glucose uptake by muscles, and reducing circulating androgen levels as well, which can support more regular ovulation and menstrual cycles.

Although metformin is not FDA-approved to treat PCOS, it's widely prescribed as an off-label treatment, particularly for those with insulin resistance or fertility difficulties, and it's backed by extensive research and clinical guidelines. Beyond helping regulate cycles and support ovulation, metformin may also help reduce androgen-related symptoms such as acne and excess hair growth, and can aid with weight management for those affected by PCOS-related weight gain.

Take metformin exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Take metformin with a meal, unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Some forms of metformin are taken only once daily with the evening meal. Follow your doctor's instructions.
Take immediate release tablets in divided doses 2 to 3 times a day with meals. Your dose will be increased slowly to minimise gastrointestinal side effects.
Do not crush, chew, or break an extended-release tablet. Swallow it whole.
Measure liquid medicine carefully. Shake the oral suspension before you measure a dose. Use the dosing syringe provided, or use a medicine dose-measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Some tablets are made with a shell that is not absorbed or melted in the body. Part of this shell may appear in your stool. This is normal and will not make the medicine less effective.

You may have low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) and feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, confused, anxious, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink a fast-acting source of sugar (fruit juice, hard candy, crackers, raisins, or non-diet soda).
Your doctor may prescribe a glucagon injection kit in case you have severe hypoglycemia. Be sure your family or close friends know how to give you this injection in an emergency.
Blood sugar levels can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals. Ask your doctor before changing your dose or medication schedule.
Metformin is only part of a complete treatment program that may also include diet, exercise, weight control, regular blood sugar testing, and special medical care. Follow your doctor's instructions very closely.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Your doctor may have you take extra vitamin B12 while you are taking this medicine. Take only the amount of vitamin B12 that your doctor has prescribed.

Extended-release tablets:
