Avoid use in patients with hepatic impairment.

Does metformin work for weight loss?:
Yes. Metformin can lead to a modest weight loss, though results vary, and it's generally smaller amount of weight loss than what's seen with medications specifically approved for weight loss.
In the landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomized controlled trial in people at high risk for diabetes, participants taking metformin lost more weight than those on placebo. Metformin patients lost 2.7% of body weight after one year, compared to 0.43% for placebo, and 2.1% after two years compared to essentially no change (0.02%) for placebo. Looking at it another way, 29% of people on metformin lost at least 5% of their starting body weight after one year, versus just 13% on placebo, a gap that held up at the two-year mark (26% vs. 14%).
Metformin is not FDA-approved for weight loss.

Common side effects:
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.
Less common side effects were abnormal stools, hypoglycemia, myalgia, lightheadedness, dyspnea, nail disorder, rash, increased sweating, taste disorder, chest discomfort, chills, flu syndrome, flushing, and palpitation, which occurred between 1% and less than 5% of patients.
Taking your medicine with meals can help reduce these side effects, and you may find the slow-release tablets reduce gastric side effects. Tell your doctor if the side effects bother you a lot, last for more than a few weeks, come back after they've gone away, or start later in therapy. You may need a lower dose or need to stop taking the medicine for a short period or for good.

Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) by itself. However, hypoglycemia can happen if you do not eat enough, if you drink alcohol, or if you take other medicines to lower blood sugar.
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metformin: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
This medicine can rarely cause patients to develop lactic acidosis, which can be fatal. See the “Warnings - Boxed Warning” for more details.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of liver problems, such as upper stomach pain, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools, or yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice).

Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea

- cold, especially in your arms and legs
- dizzy or lightheaded
- have a slow or irregular heartbeat
Other warnings:
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Metformin can lower your vitamin B12 levels over time. Your doctor may check your blood counts every year and your B12 levels every 2 to 3 years to catch any problems early.
Low blood sugar when taken with insulin or other diabetes medicines: Taking metformin along with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs (ones that boost insulin release) raises the risk of low blood sugar. If you're on one of these combinations, your doctor may lower the dose of the other medicine.
Macrovascular Outcomes: There have been no clinical studies that clearly show metformin reduces the risk of macrovascular disease, such as diseases or conditions that affect the coronary arteries, the aorta, and large arteries in the brain and limbs.
Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose can cause severe hypoglycemia or lactic acidosis.

Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.
Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides.
Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity. Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Many drugs can interact with metformin; this includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any medicine you start or stop using.
Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.

Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

Contrast dye used in imaging tests (like CT scans): This type of dye can temporarily affect kidney function, which can let metformin build up in your body. Your doctor may have you stop taking metformin around the time of the test and restart it once your kidney function is confirmed to be back to normal.
Avoid drinking alcohol. It lowers blood sugar and may increase your risk of lactic acidosis.

Tell your doctor if you also use opioid medicine, herbal products, or medicine for depression, mental illness, Parkinson's disease, migraine headaches, serious infections, or prevention of nausea and vomiting. An interaction with methylphenidate could cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome.
Tell your doctor if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
- depression, mental illness, bipolar disorder, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts or actions;
- blood circulation problems in the hands or feet;
- alcoholism or drug addiction; or
- if you take Adhansia - an allergy to aspirin or yellow food dye.
- phenylketonuria (PKU), as some chewable tablets contain phenylalanine.
To make sure methylphenidate is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have::
- problems with the esophagus, stomach, or intestines; or
- seizures, epilepsy, or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG).

Becoming dependent on methylphenidate during pregnancy can cause premature birth or low birth weight. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of methylphenidate on the baby.
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine. If you are breastfeeding, tell your doctor if you notice symptoms in the baby such as agitation, sleep problems, feeding problems, or reduced weight gain.
methylphenidate is not approved for use by anyone younger than 6 years old.

Take methylphenidate exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Methylphenidate may be habit-forming. Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death. Keep the medication where others cannot get to it. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
Most brands of methylphenidate are taken 1 or 2 times during the day. Jornay PM is for use only at night between 6:30 and 9:30 pm.
You may take methylphenidate with or without food, but take it the same way each time.
Swallow the extended-release capsule or tablet whole and do not crush, chew, or break it.
If you cannot swallow an extended-release CAPSULE whole, open it and mix the medicine with soft food such as applesauce, pudding or yogurt. Swallow the mixture right away WITHOUT CHEWING.

You must chew the chewable tablet well and swallow it with at least 8 ounces (a full glass) of water or other liquid to prevent choking.
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Allow the orally disintegrating tablet to dissolve in your mouth without chewing.
Apply the skin patch to your hip area 2 hours before an effect is needed and remove it within 9 hours. Do not wear the patch longer than 9 hours a day. Avoid exposing the patch to direct external heat sources, such as hair dryers, heating pads, or electric blankets.
Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery.
Your treatment may also include counseling or other treatments.
Your doctor will need to check your progress on a regular basis. Your heart and blood pressure may also need to be checked often.
Store tightly closed at room temperature, away from moisture, heat, and light. Keep your medicine in a place where no one can use it improperly.

Do not keep leftover medicine. Ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program. You may also mix the leftover medicine with cat litter or coffee grounds in a sealed plastic bag and throw the bag in the trash.

Methylphenidate may be habit-forming. Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death. Tell your doctor if you have had problems with drug or alcohol abuse.
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Methylphenidate may cause new or worsening psychosis (unusual thoughts or behavior), especially if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of heart problems - chest pain, feeling light-headed or short of breath; signs of psychosis - paranoia, aggression, new behavior problems, seeing or hearing things that are not real; signs of circulation problems - unexplained wounds on your fingers or toes.
Tell your doctor if you have a history of drug or alcohol addiction. Keep the medication where others cannot get to it.
Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of methylphenidate could be fatal.
Overdose symptoms may include nausea, dry mouth, vomiting, diarrhea, anxiety, agitation, restlessness, tremor, muscle twitches, rapid breathing, confusion, hallucinations, dilated pupils, muscle pain or weakness, fever, sweating, headache, pounding in your neck or ears, fast or pounding heartbeats, feeling light-headed, fainting, seizure (convulsions), or coma.

Methylphenidate is a central nervous system stimulant. It affects chemicals in the brain and nerves that contribute to hyperactivity and impulse control.
Methylphenidate is used to treat attention deficit disorder (ADD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and narcolepsy.
Methylphenidate should be used as a part of a total treatment program for ADHD that may include counseling or other therapies.

Avoid drinking alcohol.
Avoid driving or hazardous activity until you know how methylphenidate will affect you. Your reactions could be impaired.

Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you:
- Take any other medicine for your heart or blood pressure, especially digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, or verapamil
- Take fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, or propafenone, which raise metoprolol levels in your blood
- Are pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding
- Have liver problems
- Have ever had a severe allergic reaction to anything, including foods and insect stings
Kidney problems do not usually change your dose. The amount of metoprolol in your body and how long it lasts are not meaningfully different in people with kidney failure.

Metoprolol crosses the placenta and passes into breast milk in small amounts. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding.
Studies published to date have not shown a link between metoprolol taken in pregnancy and major birth defects or miscarriage. Reports on growth restriction, early birth, and death around the time of birth have been inconsistent, and those studies have limitations that make them hard to interpret. Untreated high blood pressure and untreated heart failure in pregnancy carry their own serious risks for both mother and baby.
Babies born to mothers taking metoprolol may have low blood pressure, low blood sugar, a slow heartbeat, or slow breathing, so they are watched after birth.
The amount of metoprolol a breastfed baby receives is estimated at 0.05 mg to under 1 mg a day, which is about 0.5% to 2% of the mother's weight-adjusted dose. No side effects in breastfed babies have been identified. Babies are still monitored for a slow heartbeat and for signs such as unusual sleepiness.

Take metoprolol at the same time each day, exactly as prescribed. Do not change your dose or stop taking it without talking to your prescriber first.
Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets should be taken with a meal or immediately after a meal. For extended-release tablets and capsules, taking your dose with or just after a meal is preferred, but food does not have a significant effect on how much metoprolol your body absorbs.
- Keep taking metoprolol even if you feel well. High blood pressure often causes no symptoms.
- Extended-release tablets are scored and can be split in half if your prescriber tells you to. Swallow the whole or half tablet without crushing or chewing it.
- Extended-release capsules (Kapspargo Sprinkle) should be swallowed whole. If you cannot swallow the capsule, you can open it and sprinkle the contents over a teaspoon of soft food such as applesauce, pudding, or yogurt. Swallow the mixture within 60 minutes and do not save any for later.
- Tell your doctor if you are fasting or vomiting, because this raises your risk of low blood sugar.

- Your blood pressure and heart rate will need checking regularly.
- Store metoprolol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C), away from moisture and heat.
Metoprolol injection is given into a vein by a healthcare professional in a coronary care unit or similar setting, where your blood pressure, heart rate, and heart tracing can be watched. You are then switched to metoprolol tablets.

The usual starting dose is 25 mg to 100 mg once a day for extended-release metoprolol, and 100 mg a day for immediate-release metoprolol. Your dose is then adjusted at intervals of a week or longer until your blood pressure or symptoms are controlled.
Metoprolol tartrate (immediate-release tablets) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 100 mg a day, as one dose or split into two | 100 mg to 450 mg a day. Doses above 450 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg a day, split into two doses | 100 mg to 400 mg a day. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
After a heart attack | 50 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours, starting 15 minutes after the last dose given into a vein. If the full intravenous dose was not tolerated, 25 mg is used. | Maintenance is 100 mg twice a day, continued for at least 3 months.
With immediate-release tablets, a once-daily dose may not keep blood pressure controlled for the full 24 hours, especially at 100 mg. Splitting the dose or taking a larger daily dose may be needed.

Metoprolol succinate (extended-release tablets and capsules) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 25 mg to 100 mg once a day | Adjust weekly or less often. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg once a day | Increase weekly until symptoms are controlled or your heart rate slows noticeably. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Heart failure | 25 mg once a day for two weeks, or 12.5 mg once a day in more severe heart failure | Double the dose every two weeks to the highest dose you tolerate, up to 200 mg once a day.
Kapspargo Sprinkle capsules are not suitable to start heart failure treatment if a dose below 25 mg is needed.
Metoprolol dosage for children:

Extended-release metoprolol is the only form approved for children, and only for high blood pressure in children aged 6 years and older. The starting dose is 1 mg for each kilogram of body weight once a day, up to a maximum first dose of 50 mg. Doses above 2 mg/kg, or above 200 mg a day, have not been studied. Extended-release metoprolol has not been studied in children under 6 years.
Dose adjustments:
- Liver problems. Start at a lower dose than usual and increase slowly.
- Kidney problems. No dose reduction is needed.
- Older adults. A low starting dose is generally used, because liver, kidney, and heart function are more often reduced and other medicines are more often involved.
- Switching between forms. When changing from immediate-release to extended-release metoprolol, the same total daily dose is used.

The most common side effects of metoprolol are tiredness, dizziness, low mood (depression), diarrhea, shortness of breath, a slow heartbeat (bradycardia), and itching or rash. Most side effects reported in studies were mild and did not last.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metoprolol: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Common side effects of metoprolol:
In studies of people taking metoprolol for high blood pressure or angina:
- Tiredness and dizziness occurred in about 10% of people
- Low mood or depression was reported in about 5 out of 100 people
- Diarrhea occurred in about 5% of people
- Itching or rash occurred in about 5% of people
- Shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat occurred in about 3% of people
- Cold hands and feet, palpitations, swelling of the ankles, and low blood pressure were each reported in about 1% of people
- Nausea, dry mouth, stomach pain, constipation, gas, and heartburn were each reported in about 1% of people

Headache, nightmares, trouble sleeping, confusion, and short-term memory loss have also been reported.
In the heart failure study of extended-release metoprolol, dizziness or vertigo was reported by 1.8% of people taking metoprolol compared with 1.0% taking placebo, and a slow heartbeat by 1.5% compared with 0.4%.
Other reported side effects:
These have been reported since metoprolol came on the market. Their frequency is not known:
- Hair thinning or hair loss, which reversed after stopping
- Reduced sex drive and difficulty getting an erection
- Dry eyes, blurred vision, and ringing in the ears
- Sweating, sensitivity to sunlight, and worsening of psoriasis
- Change in taste, joint and muscle pain, and fainting
- Liver inflammation (hepatitis)
- A severe drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), which can show up as fever, chills, or a sore throat
Serious side effects of metoprolol:
Some of these, such as shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat, are also listed as common side effects above. They need urgent attention when they are severe, new, or getting worse.

Call your doctor at once if you have:
- A very slow heartbeat, pauses in your heartbeat, or a feeling that you might faint. Sinus pause, heart block, and cardiac arrest have all been reported.
- Signs that heart failure is getting worse, such as weight gain over a few days, more shortness of breath, or swelling of your feet or lower legs
- Wheezing or trouble breathing
- Chest pain that is worse or more frequent than usual, especially if you have recently stopped or missed doses
- Cold, pale, or blue fingers and toes, or pain in your legs when you walk
- Confusion, hallucinations, or memory problems
- Yellowing of your skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver inflammation
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack. If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond. This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.
Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you.
- Asthma or other breathing problems. Beta blockers can tighten the airways. Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand.
- Heart failure. Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased. Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness.
- A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart. This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Your heart rate should be monitored.

- Diabetes or long gaps without food. Metoprolol can hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, and can make low blood sugar more severe or last longer. The risk is higher if you are fasting, not eating regularly, or vomiting.
- An overactive thyroid. Metoprolol can mask signs of an overactive thyroid. Stopping it suddenly can trigger a thyroid crisis.
- Circulation problems in your arms or legs. Beta blockers can make symptoms of poor circulation worse.
- A history of severe allergic reactions. If you have anaphylaxis while taking a beta blocker, the usual dose of injectable epinephrine may not work as well.
- Pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal gland). Metoprolol must only be started after an alpha blocker has been started, or blood pressure can rise sharply.
- Liver disease. Metoprolol is broken down by the liver, so levels can build up. Treatment is usually started at a lower dose.

Surgery. Tell your surgeon and dentist that you take metoprolol. Long-term beta blocker treatment is not usually stopped before surgery. Starting a high dose of extended-release metoprolol shortly before non-cardiac surgery is avoided, because in one large trial this was linked to more slow heartbeats, low blood pressure, strokes, and deaths.
Skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once and do not double up to catch up.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Too much metoprolol can cause a dangerously slow heartbeat, very low blood pressure, and cardiogenic shock. It can also cause heart block, heart failure, wheezing, low oxygen levels, drowsiness or loss of consciousness, nausea, and vomiting. Overdose is treated in an intensive care setting. Dialysis does not remove metoprolol effectively.

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)

- Metoprolol succinate, an extended-release tablet or capsule taken once a day (brand names Toprol-XL and Kapspargo Sprinkle)
Metoprolol tartrate is also given as an injection into a vein in a hospital during a heart attack.

Metoprolol is FDA-approved to treat high blood pressure, angina, heart failure, and heart attack, but the two forms are not approved for the same conditions.
Condition | Metoprolol tartrate (immediate release) | Metoprolol succinate (extended release)
High blood pressure (hypertension) in adults | Yes | Yes
High blood pressure in children 6 years and older | No | Yes
Angina (chest pain) | Yes | Yes
Heart failure | No | Yes
Heart attack (myocardial infarction) | Yes | No
High blood pressure (hypertension). Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal heart and blood vessel events, mainly strokes and heart attacks. Metoprolol can be used on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Many people need more than one medicine to reach their blood pressure goal.
Angina. Metoprolol is used for long-term treatment of angina, to reduce how often attacks happen and to help you do more before chest pain starts. It is not used to stop an attack that has already begun.

Heart failure. Only the extended-release form is approved for heart failure. It is used to reduce the risk of dying from heart and blood vessel causes and to reduce hospital admissions for heart failure.
Heart attack (myocardial infarction). Metoprolol tartrate is used in people whose blood pressure and circulation are stable after a definite or suspected heart attack, to reduce the risk of dying from heart and blood vessel causes. In hospital, it may be started as an injection into a vein and then continued as tablets.

The two forms release the same medicine at different speeds, and they are approved for different conditions. Metoprolol tartrate is released all at once, so it acts sooner and wears off sooner. Metoprolol succinate is released slowly over the day, so one dose lasts about 24 hours. Only the extended-release form is approved for heart failure and for children, and only the immediate-release form is approved for use after a heart attack.
Metoprolol tartrate | Metoprolol succinate
Release | Immediate release | Extended release
Usual dosing | Once or twice a day, or every 6 hours after a heart attack | Once a day
Forms | Tablet, injection | Tablet, capsule
Tablet strengths | 25 mg, 37.5 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg | 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg
Brand names | Lopressor | Toprol-XL, Kapspargo Sprinkle
Approved for heart failure | No | Yes
Approved after a heart attack | Yes | No
Approved for children 6 years and older | No | Yes
If you switch from immediate-release metoprolol to the extended-release form, the total amount you take in a day stays the same. Your prescriber makes this change, not you.

The interactions that matter most are medicines that also slow the heart and medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which raises metoprolol levels in your blood.
- Digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, and verapamil. These all slow the heart's electrical signal and heart rate. Taking them with metoprolol raises the risk of a very slow heartbeat.
- Clonidine, when stopping either medicine. If you take both, the metoprolol is stopped several days before clonidine is slowly withdrawn, because beta blockers can worsen the blood pressure rebound that follows clonidine withdrawal.
- Quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and propafenone. These strong CYP2D6 blockers double the amount of metoprolol in your blood. Quinidine tripled levels of one form of metoprolol and doubled how long it lasted. Weaker CYP2D6 blockers are likely to raise levels too.
- Reserpine and MAO inhibitors. These deplete adrenaline-type chemicals and can add to metoprolol's effect, causing low blood pressure or a marked slowing of the heart.

- Epinephrine. If you need epinephrine for a severe allergic reaction, the usual dose may not work as well while you are on a beta blocker.
- Other medicines that lower blood pressure or heart rate, including fingolimod, can add to metoprolol's effect.
Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here.

- Avoid driving and other tasks that need alertness until you know how metoprolol affects you. It can make you feel tired or less alert.
- Get up slowly from sitting or lying down, because metoprolol can make you feel dizzy or lightheaded.
- Avoid alcohol if you take Kapspargo Sprinkle capsules. Alcohol makes the capsule release its metoprolol much faster, which raises the risk of side effects.
- Do not stop taking metoprolol on your own, even if you feel fine.

You should not take metoprolol if you have a very slow heart rate, heart block beyond the first degree, sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker, cardiogenic shock, or heart failure that is not under control.
Metoprolol is not for you if you have:
- Severe bradycardia (a very slow heart rate)
- Second-degree or third-degree heart block, which is a fault in the heart's electrical signal
- Sick sinus syndrome, unless you have a permanent pacemaker
- Cardiogenic shock, when the heart cannot pump enough blood
- Decompensated heart failure, meaning heart failure that is not stable
- An allergy to metoprolol or to any of the other ingredients in your product
Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets should also not be used if your top blood pressure reading is below 100 mmHg.

You should not use montelukast if you are allergic to it.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- mental illness or psychosis; or
- asthma, or a history of severe allergic reaction (sneezing, runny or stuffy nose, wheezing, shortness of breath) after taking aspirin or another NSAID.
The chewable montelukast tablet may contain phenylalanine and could be harmful if you have phenylketonuria (PKU).
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
Do not give this medicine to a child without a doctor's advice.

Take montelukast exactly as prescribed by your doctor and read all medication guides or instruction sheets about montelukast.
Montelukast is not a fast-acting rescue medicine for asthma attacks. Seek medical attention if your breathing problems get worse quickly, or if you think your medications are not working.
Montelukast is usually taken once every evening, with or without food.
For exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, take a single dose at least 2 hours before exercise, and do not take another dose for at least 24 hours.
Swallow the regular tablet whole, with a glass of water.
You must chew the chewable tablet before you swallow it.
Place the oral granules directly in your mouth and swallow, or mix them with applesauce, mashed carrots, rice, or ice cream. The granules may also be mixed with baby formula or breast milk. Do not use any other type of liquid. Use the mixture within 15 minutes. Do not save for later use.

If you also use an oral steroid medication, you should not stop using it suddenly when you start taking montelukast. Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose.
Do not change your dose or stop using asthma medication without your doctor's advice.
Store montelukast at room temperature away from moisture and heat. Do not open a packet of montelukast oral granules until you are ready to use them.

- cold symptoms such as runny or stuffy nose, sinus pain, cough, sore throat.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Stop taking montelukast and call your doctor right away if you have any unusual changes in mood or behavior (such as agitation, confusion, depression, sleep problems, compulsive behaviors, hallucinations, or suicidal thoughts or actions).
Tell your doctor right away if you have signs of blood vessel inflammation: flu-like symptoms, severe sinus pain, a skin rash, numbness or a "pins and needles" feeling in your arms or legs.
If you miss a dose of montelukast, skip the missed dose and use your next dose at the regular time. Do not use two doses at one time.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.

Montelukast helps to reduce inflammation and may be used to prevent asthma attacks in adults and children at least 2 years old.
Montelukast is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (a narrowing of the air passages in the lungs due to exercise that is also known as exercise-induced asthma) in adults and children who are at least 6 years old.
For adults and children at least 2 years old with symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinitis, and people over 6 months old with perennial (year-round) allergies, montelukast may be considered when other treatments have not worked.
If you already take montelukast regularly to prevent asthma or allergy symptoms, do not take an extra dose to treat exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
Montelukast is not a fast-acting rescue medicine for asthma attacks and needs to be taken daily to work properly.
Montelukast was FDA-approved in 1998.
Other drugs may affect montelukast, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you use.

Avoid situations or activities that may trigger an asthma attack.
If your asthma symptoms get worse when you take aspirin, avoid taking aspirin or other NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), celecoxib, diclofenac, indomethacin, meloxicam, and others.

You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
- high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
- high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or
- any condition that makes it hard for your body to absorb nutrients from food (malabsorption).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease;
- kidney disease; or
- an electrolyte imbalance.
Certain forms of ergocalciferol may contain ingredients you should know about, such as peanut or soybean oil, sugar, aspartame (phenylalanine), or certain food dyes. Ask a doctor before using ergocalciferol if you have allergies, diabetes, or phenylketonuria (PKU).
Too much vitamin D could harm an unborn baby, and your dose needs may be different during pregnancy. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or if you become pregnant while taking ergocalciferol.
Ergocalciferol can pass into breast milk and may cause side effects in the nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding.
Do not give ergocalciferol to a child without medical advice. Your child's dose will depend on age, weight, diet, and other factors.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop taking ergocalciferol and call your doctor at once if you have:
- chest pain, feeling short of breath;
- growth problems (in a child taking ergocalciferol); or
- early signs of vitamin D overdose --weakness, metallic taste in your mouth, weight loss, muscle or bone pain, constipation, nausea, and vomiting.
Less serious side effects may be more likely, and you may have none at all.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Omeprazole usually takes 1 to 4 days of once-daily dosing to reach its full effect, and some people get complete relief of their symptoms within 24 hours. It begins reducing stomach acid within about 1 hour of the first dose, but it is not designed to relieve heartburn right away.
What to expect after you start taking omeprazole:
- Within 1 hour: omeprazole starts to reduce acid production in your stomach
- Around 2 hours: a single dose reaches its strongest acid-lowering effect
- Within 24 hours: some people get complete relief of their symptoms
- 1 to 4 days: most people feel the full benefit
- About 4 days: the acid-lowering effect reaches its maximum with once-daily dosing
How fast does omeprazole start working?:
Omeprazole starts working within about 1 hour, and a single dose has its strongest effect at around 2 hours. This is when the medicine begins lowering acid production, which is not the same as when your heartburn or acid reflux symptoms stop.

Omeprazole does not work immediately on symptoms you are already feeling. It is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), which means it reduces how much acid your stomach makes rather than neutralizing acid that is already there.

Take omeprazole exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Use Prilosec OTC (over-the-counter) exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor.

Some conditions are treated with a combination of omeprazole and antibiotics. Use all medications as directed.
This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

Omeprazole is not to be used for the immediate relief of heartburn symptoms.

Omeprazole is used to treat excess stomach acid in conditions such as stomach ulcers, heartburn or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), active duodenal ulcer, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and erosive esophagitis.
Omeprazole may also be given together with antibiotics to treat gastric ulcers caused by infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), in adult patients.
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that works by blocking the acid pump in your stomach, reducing how much acid it makes and giving irritated or damaged tissue a chance to heal.
Omeprazole brand names are Prilosec, Prilosec OTC, and generic brands are available.
Omeprazole is available over the counter (OTC) and as a prescription medication.

Over-the-counter omeprazole is used for:
- frequent heartburn that occurs 2 or more days a week in adults 18 years and older
- It is taken as a 14-day course, once a day for 14 days in a row. It may take 1 to 4 days to reach its full effect, so it is not used for immediate relief of symptoms. Do not take it for longer than 14 days, and do not start another 14-day course within 4 months, unless your doctor tells you to.
Prescription omeprazole can be used for:
- active duodenal ulcer (a sore in the first part of the small intestine) in adults
- Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection in adults, taken together with antibiotics, to reduce the risk of a duodenal ulcer coming back
- active benign gastric ulcer (a non-cancerous sore in the stomach lining) in adults
- symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), such as heartburn, in adults and children 1 year of age and older
- erosive esophagitis (EE) caused by acid reflux in adults and children 1 month of age and older
- keeping erosive esophagitis healed after treatment, in adults and children 1 year of age and older
- pathological hypersecretory conditions (conditions in which the stomach makes too much acid) in adults, including Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Omeprazole can cause diarrhea, which may be a sign of a new infection. If you have diarrhea that is watery or bloody, call your doctor before using anti-diarrhea medicine.

- a blockage in your digestive tract (stomach or intestines).
Ondansetron is not expected to harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant.
It is not known whether ondansetron passes into breast milk or if it could harm a nursing baby. Tell your doctor if you are breast-feeding a baby.
Ondansetron is not approved for use by anyone younger than 1 month old.
Ondansetron orally disintegrating tablets may contain phenylalanine. Tell your doctor if you have phenylketonuria (PKU).
Usual Adult Dose of Ondansetron for Nausea/Vomiting -- Chemotherapy Induced:

Oral: Highly Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (HEC): -Recommended dose: 24 mg orally 30 minutes before the start of single-day HEC (including cisplatin doses of 50 mg/m2 or greater) Moderately Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (MEC): -Recommended dose: 8 mg orally twice a day, with the first dose administered 30 minutes before the start of chemotherapy and the subsequent dose 8 hours later; then 8 mg orally 2 times a day (every 12 hours) for 1 to 2 days after the completion of chemotherapy Parenteral: -Recommended dose: 0.15 mg/kg IV, with the first dose (infused over 15 minutes) 30 minutes before the start of emetogenic chemotherapy and subsequent doses given 4 and 8 hours after the first dose. -Maximum dose: 16 mg per dose Comments: -Multi-day, single-dose administration of 24 mg orally for HEC has not been studied. -The injection formulation should be diluted prior to IV administration. Uses: -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with HEC or MEC -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with initial and repeat courses of emetogenic chemotherapy

Oral: Highly Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (HEC): -Recommended dose: 24 mg orally 30 minutes before the start of single-day HEC (including cisplatin doses of 50 mg/m2 or greater) Moderately Emetogenic Cancer Chemotherapy (MEC): -Recommended dose: 8 mg orally twice a day, with the first dose administered 30 minutes before the start of chemotherapy and the subsequent dose 8 hours later; then 8 mg orally 2 times a day (every 12 hours) for 1 to 2 days after the completion of chemotherapy Parenteral: -Recommended dose: 0.15 mg/kg IV, with the first dose (infused over 15 minutes) 30 minutes before the start of emetogenic chemotherapy and subsequent doses given 4 and 8 hours after the first dose. -Maximum dose: 16 mg per dose Comments: -Multi-day, single-dose administration of 24 mg orally for HEC has not been studied. -The injection formulation should be diluted prior to IV administration. Uses: -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with HEC or MEC -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with initial and repeat courses of emetogenic chemotherapy

Usual Adult Dose of Ondansetron for Nausea/Vomiting -- Postoperative:
Oral: -Recommended dose: 16 mg orally 1 hour before the induction of anesthesia Parenteral: -Recommended dose: 4 mg IV (undiluted) immediately before induction of anesthesia or postoperatively (nausea and/or vomiting within 2 hours after surgery) -Alternative route: 4 mg IM (undiluted) Comment: -Administration of a second dose does not provide additional control of nausea and vomiting. Use: -Prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting
Usual Adult Dose for Nausea/Vomiting--Radiation Induced:

Recommended dose: 8 mg orally 3 times a day -Total Body Irradiation: 8 mg orally 1 to 2 hours before each fraction of radiotherapy administered each day -Single High-dose Fraction Radiotherapy to the Abdomen: 8 mg orally 1 to 2 hours before radiotherapy, with subsequent doses every 8 hours after the first dose for 1 to 2 days after the completion of radiotherapy -Daily Fractionated Radiotherapy to the Abdomen: 8 mg orally 1 to 2 hours before radiotherapy, with subsequent doses every 8 hours after the first dose for each day radiotherapy is given Use: -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with radiotherapy, either as total body irradiation, single high-dose fraction, or daily fractions to the abdomen
Usual Pediatric Dose for Nausea/Vomiting -- Postoperative:

Parenteral: 1 month to 12 years: Less than 40 kg: -Recommended dose: 0.1 mg/kg IV over 2 to 5 minutes immediately prior to/following anesthesia induction or postoperatively (nausea and/or vomiting occurring shortly after surgery) 40 kg and greater: -Recommended dose: 4 mg IV over 2 to 5 minutes immediately prior to/following anesthesia induction or postoperatively (nausea and/or vomiting occurring shortly after surgery) Use: -Prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting
Usual Pediatric Dose for Nausea/Vomiting -- Chemotherapy Induced:

Oral: 4 to 11 years: -Recommended dose: 4 mg orally 3 times a day, with the first dose administered 30 minutes before the start of chemotherapy, and subsequent doses 4 and 8 hours after the first dose; then 4 mg orally 3 times a day (every 8 hours) for 1 to 2 days after the completion of chemotherapy 12 years and older: -Recommended dose: 8 mg orally twice a day, with the first dose administered 30 minutes before the start of chemotherapy and the subsequent dose 8 hours later; then 8 mg orally 2 times a day (every 12 hours) for 1 to 2 days after the completion of chemotherapy Parenteral: 6 months to 18 years: -Recommended dose: 0.15 mg/kg IV, with the first dose (infused over 15 minutes) 30 minutes before the start of emetogenic chemotherapy, and subsequent doses given 4 and 8 hours after the first dose -Maximum dose: 16 mg (per dose) Comments: -The injection formulation should be diluted in 50 mL prior to IV administration. -This drug should be used to prevent nausea and vomiting associated with moderately to highly emetogenic chemotherapy.

Uses: -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with moderately emetogenic cancer chemotherapy -Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with initial and repeat courses of emetogenic chemotherapy

Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.
Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. Skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. Do not take extra medicine to make up the missed dose.

Ondansetron blocks the actions of chemicals in the body that can trigger nausea and vomiting.
Ondansetron is used to prevent nausea and vomiting that may be caused by surgery, cancer chemotherapy, or radiation treatment.

Taking ondansetron while you are using certain other medicines can cause high levels of serotonin to build up in your body, a condition called "serotonin syndrome," which can be fatal. Tell your doctor if you also use:

- a narcotic (opioid) medication; or

Usual Adult Dose for Erosive Esophagitis:
Treatment of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day for up to 8 weeks; however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment. Safety and efficacy beyond 16 weeks of therapy have not been established. Maintenance of Healing of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day. Controlled studies have been limited to 12 months of pantoprazole therapy.
Usual Adult Dose for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease:
Parenteral: 40 mg once a day for 7 to 10 days, administered via intravenous infusion over a period of 15 minutes. Intravenous therapy should be discontinued as soon as the patient is able to resume oral therapy. Oral: 40 mg orally once a day, for short-term administration (up to 8 weeks); however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment. Safety and efficacy beyond 16 weeks of therapy have not been established.
Usual Adult Dose for Duodenal Ulcer:

Study (n=54) 40 mg orally once a day, dose was increased every 12 weeks by 40 mg increments to a maximum of 120 mg per day, for 28 weeks. Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete duodenal ulcer healing in up to 87% and 94% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.
Usual Adult Dose for Gastric Ulcer:
40 mg orally once a day. Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete gastric ulcer healing in up to 87% and 97% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.
Usual Adult Dose for Helicobacter pylori Infection:

Study (n=242) - Triple therapy: 40 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, commonly in conjunction with clarithromycin and either amoxicillin or metronidazole to eradicate Helicobacter pylori, followed with 40 mg pantoprazole orally once daily until day 28. Triple therapy has resulted in eradication rates of greater than 95%. The QUADRATE Study (n=405) - Quadruple therapy: 40 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, concomitantly with bismuth subcitrate and tetracycline, both four times daily, and metronidazole 200 mg three times daily and 400 mg at bedtime. Helicobacter Pylori eradication was achieved in 82% of patients.
Usual Adult Dose for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome:
Parenteral: 80 mg every 12 hours, administered by 15-minute infusion. Daily doses higher than 240 mg administered in equally divided doses by 15-minute infusion, or administered for more than 6 days have not been studied. Oral: 40 mg twice daily, to a maximum of 240 mg per day. Some patients have received treatment with pantoprazole for more than 2 years.
Usual Adult Dose for Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis:

Study (n=21) - Stress Ulcer bleeding prophylaxis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg twice daily, as a bolus infusion over a period of 15 minutes, to a maximum daily dose of 240 mg, divided into three equal doses. Study (n=20) - Peptic Ulcer rebleeding prophylaxis after hemostasis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg IV bolus, followed by continuous infusion of 8 mg/hr for 3 days, after which therapy may be continued with an oral PPI.
Usual Adult Dose for Peptic Ulcer:
Study (n=21) - Stress Ulcer bleeding prophylaxis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg twice daily, as a bolus infusion over a period of 15 minutes, to a maximum daily dose of 240 mg, divided into three equal doses. Study (n=20) - Peptic Ulcer rebleeding prophylaxis after hemostasis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg IV bolus, followed by continuous infusion of 8 mg/hr for 3 days, after which therapy may be continued with an oral PPI.

Take potassium chloride exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or with a special dose-measuring spoon or medicine cup. If you do not have a dose-measuring device, ask your pharmacist for one.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on a tablet or capsule. Sucking on the pill could irritate your mouth or throat.
Call your doctor if you have trouble swallowing a potassium chloride capsule or tablet. You may be able to dissolve the tablet in water, or mix the medicine from a capsule with soft food. Carefully follow your doctor's instructions.

Mix the powder form of this medicine with at least 4 ounces (one-half cup) of cold water or fruit juice before taking. Drink the mixture slowly, over 5 to 10 minutes in all. To make sure you get the entire dose, add a little more water to the same glass, swirl gently and drink right away.
To be sure this medicine is helping your condition, you may need frequent blood tests. You may not notice any change in your symptoms, but your blood work will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium chloride. Your heart function may need to be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG). Even if you have no symptoms, tests can help your doctor determine if this medicine is effective.
Your treatment may include a special diet. Follow the diet plan created for you by your doctor or nutrition counselor. Get familiar with the list of foods you should eat or avoid to help control your condition.

Potassium-rich foods include: squash, baked potatoes (skin on), spinach, lentils, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, zucchini, kidney or navy beans, raisins, watermelon, orange juice, bananas, cantaloupe, and low-fat milk or yogurt. Consume only the daily amounts recommended by your doctor or nutrition counselor.
Some tablets are made with a shell that is not absorbed or melted in the body. Part of this shell may appear in your stool. This is normal and will not make the medicine less effective.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat. Keep the medication in a closed container.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
- severe throat irritation;
- stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
- high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
- signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
- gas, stomach pain; or
- the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia), or if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition, your blood may need to be tested often. Your heart rate may also be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG) to measure electrical activity of the heart. This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness or limp feeling, severe stomach pain, and numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor. If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.

Do not crush, chew, or suck on an extended-release tablet or capsule. Swallow the pill whole unless your doctor or pharmacist tells you your specific tablet can be broken. Crushing or chewing the pill may cause too much of the drug to be released at one time. Sucking on a tablet can irritate your mouth or throat. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. Skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. Do not take extra medicine to make up the missed dose.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Overdose symptoms may include irregular heartbeats, chest pain, or muscle weakness.

Potassium is a mineral that is found in many foods and is needed for several functions of your body, especially the beating of your heart.
Potassium chloride is used to prevent or to treat low blood levels of potassium (hypokalemia).
Potassium levels can be low as a result of a disease or from taking certain medicines, or after a prolonged illness with diarrhea or vomiting.

Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any you start or stop using, especially:
- a diuretic or "water pill"; or
- heart or blood pressure medication.
- NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, celecoxib, diclofenac, indomethacin, or meloxicam.
This list is not complete. Other drugs may interact with potassium chloride, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed in this medication guide.

Avoid taking supplements or using other products that contain potassium without first asking your doctor. Salt substitutes or low-salt dietary products often contain potassium. If you take certain products together you may accidentally get too much potassium. Read the label of any other medicine you are using to see if it contains potassium.

Long-term steroid use can cause bone loss. Your risk is higher if you smoke, if you do not exercise, if you do not get enough calcium or vitamin D, or if osteoporosis runs in your family. Talk with your doctor about protecting your bones.
Pregnancy:
Prednisone crosses the placenta. Taking it in the first trimester may raise the risk of birth defects, and taking higher doses later in pregnancy may affect the baby's growth and their adrenal glands. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Some conditions still need steroid treatment during pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than stopping on your own.
Breastfeeding:
Prednisone passes into breast milk in small amounts. Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding so you can talk through the dose and the timing of feeds.
Children:
Prednisone is used in children, but long courses can slow growth and affect bone development. The dose should not be higher than prescribed, and your child should be monitored during treatment.
Older adults:

Older adults are more likely to have liver, kidney, or heart problems that affect how prednisone is handled, and are more likely to already have osteoporosis, diabetes, or high blood pressure. A lower dose may be needed.

Take prednisone exactly as prescribed, with food or milk to protect your stomach. Your doctor will often start you on a higher dose and then lower it. Do not change your dose or stop the medicine without advice.
- Take your dose in the morning if your doctor tells you to. Your adrenal glands are most active between 2 am and 8 am, and taking a steroid at that time interferes with them the least. A morning dose may also help you sleep better, though that is a separate benefit.
- Swallow delayed-release tablets whole. Do not crush, break, or chew them.
- Measure liquid prednisone with a marked oral syringe, dosing spoon or medicine cup, not a kitchen spoon. Use the dropper that comes with the concentrated solution.
- You may mix the concentrated solution with juice or a soft food such as applesauce.
- Tell your doctor if you have a serious illness, a fever, an infection, surgery, or a medical emergency. You may need a higher dose for a short time.
- You may need regular blood tests, blood pressure checks and eye checks during long-term treatment.

- Wear a medical alert tag or carry a card saying you take a steroid.
- Store prednisone at room temperature, away from moisture and heat. Throw away any unused concentrated solution 90 days after you first open the bottle.

Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.

The effect lasts longer than the drug itself. A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands for about one and a quarter to one and a half days, which is why prednisone is described as short-acting compared with steroids such as dexamethasone. This is also why a course of prednisone can affect your blood sugar, your sleep, and your energy for longer than the drug is measurable in your blood.
Why has my doctor prescribed prednisone every other day?:
Alternate day dosing means taking twice your usual daily dose every other morning instead of a dose every day. It is used for people who need steroid treatment for a long time. Giving your body a day off from the steroid lets your adrenal glands recover between doses, which reduces the risk of adrenal suppression, Cushing's syndrome, withdrawal symptoms, and slowed growth in children.

The trade-off is that your symptoms may flare a little late in the day you do not take it. Tell your doctor if this happens, since other treatment can often be added for that gap. Do not switch yourself to an every other day schedule, and do not double up on a day you were not meant to take a dose.
What is the difference between prednisone and prednisolone?:
Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work, while prednisolone is already in the active form. For most people the two work in a very similar way at equivalent doses. Prednisolone is often chosen for people with significant liver disease, and for children, because it comes in liquid forms that are easier to dose.
Does prednisone cause weight gain?:

Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone. It happens for two reasons. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks, and it increases appetite, which adds body fat over longer courses. It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist. Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop, but weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.
Can you drink alcohol while taking prednisone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and prednisone, but drinking is best kept to a minimum. Both irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. Alcohol also raises blood sugar and weakens bones, and prednisone does both of these too. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for you, especially if you are on a long course.
Can you take ibuprofen with prednisone?:

It is usually best to avoid ibuprofen while you are taking prednisone. Ibuprofen is an NSAID, and taking an NSAID with a steroid raises the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. The same applies to naproxen, diclofenac, and regular doses of aspirin. If you need a painkiller, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you take Tylenol with prednisone?:
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) does not interact with prednisone and does not irritate the stomach, so it is generally the preferred choice for pain or fever while you are taking prednisone. Stay within the recommended daily limit on the packet and check whether any other product you take already contains acetaminophen.
Why does prednisone keep me awake?:
Prednisone acts like your body's stress hormone, which naturally peaks in the morning to help you wake up. Taking it, especially later in the day, can leave you feeling wired, restless or unable to sleep. Taking your dose in the morning often helps. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does prednisone raise blood pressure?:

It can. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which raises blood pressure in some people, particularly at higher doses or on longer courses. Your blood pressure should be checked during treatment, and your doctor may ask you to reduce salt in your diet.
What is considered a high dose of prednisone?:
There is no official cutoff, but doctors generally treat doses under 7.5 mg a day as low, 7.5 mg to 40 mg a day as moderate, and more than 40 mg a day as high. A dose of 20 mg a day sits in the moderate range. What matters as much as the number is how long you take it, because side effects build up over time.
Can prednisone make you tired?:
Yes. Some people feel energized on prednisone while others feel drained. Poor sleep, mood changes and muscle weakness all contribute. Tiredness that starts as your dose is being lowered, or after you stop, can be a sign that your adrenal glands have not caught up yet, so tell your doctor if it is severe or comes with dizziness, nausea, or body aches.

Common prednisone side effects:
The most common prednisone side effects are trouble sleeping, mood changes, increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention and swelling, increased sweating, acne, thinning skin that bruises easily, slow wound healing, higher blood sugar, indigestion and stomach upset.
Many of these effects are dose related. They are more likely on higher doses and on longer courses, and most settle after the medicine is stopped.
Serious prednisone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to prednisone: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of infection, such as fever, chills, sore throat, cough or a wound that is not healing, since prednisone can hide the usual warning signs;
- blurred vision, eye pain or seeing halos around lights, which can be signs of glaucoma (raised pressure in the eye) or cataracts;

- flat, painless spots that are red or purple on light skin, or bluish, brown or black on dark skin, which can be a sign of Kaposi's sarcoma.
Prednisone side effects in women:
Women taking prednisone may notice irregular or missed periods, unwanted facial hair growth, acne and changes in body fat, such as a rounder face and more fat around the neck and waist. Long courses of prednisone also raise the risk of osteoporosis (thinning of the bones), and postmenopausal women are already at higher risk. Ask your doctor whether you need a bone density scan or a calcium and vitamin D supplement.
Long-term prednisone side effects:
Taking prednisone for months or years raises the risk of osteoporosis and broken bones, muscle weakness and muscle loss, cataracts and glaucoma, diabetes, high blood pressure, Cushing's syndrome (a set of changes caused by too much steroid, including a rounded face and fat around the trunk), and adrenal suppression, where your body stops making enough of its own steroid hormones.

Children who take prednisone for a long time may grow more slowly. Your child's doctor should check their growth at regular visits.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take prednisone if you have a systemic fungal infection, which is a fungal infection that has spread through your body.
Prednisone weakens your immune system. This makes it easier to get an infection; an existing infection may become worse and can reactivate an old infection, such as tuberculosis or hepatitis B. It can also hide the usual signs of infection, so an infection may be advanced before you notice it. Tell your doctor about any illness or infection you have had in the past few weeks.
Stay away from people who are sick. Chickenpox and measles can be serious or even fatal in someone taking a steroid. Call your doctor straight away if you are exposed to either one.
Do not have a live vaccine while you are taking prednisone unless your doctor says it is safe.
Do not stop taking prednisone suddenly after more than a few days of treatment. Your body needs time to start making its own steroid hormones again. Your doctor will lower your dose in steps.

Call your doctor at once if you have shortness of breath, severe pain in your upper stomach, bloody or black stools, severe depression, changes in personality or behavior, vision problems, or eye pain.

Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. Skip it if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take extra medicine to make up a missed dose. If you take prednisone once every other day, or you are following a taper, call your doctor or pharmacist for advice rather than guessing.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
A single large dose of prednisone is not likely to cause life-threatening symptoms. The bigger risk comes from taking high doses over a long time, which can cause thinning skin, easy bruising, changes in the shape or location of body fat, acne, extra facial hair, irregular periods, and loss of interest in sex.

Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders. Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies, asthma and COPD flare-ups, rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands. Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones. Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).
Prednisone belongs to the drug class called glucocorticoids, which are a type of corticosteroid.

Prednisone tablets come in 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, and 50 mg strengths. Prednisone 20 mg and prednisone 10 mg tablets are the strengths most often used for short courses in adults. Prednisone also comes as a delayed-release tablet (Rayos), as an oral liquid, and as a concentrated oral solution (Prednisone Intensol) that is measured with a special dropper.
Many of the original brands are discontinued; however, generic prednisone is available.

The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.

If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.
Prednisone formulations:
- Prednisone 1 mg tablets
- Prednisone 2.5 mg tablets

- Prednisone 5 mg tablets
- Prednisone 10 mg tablets
- Prednisone 20 mg tablets
- Prednisone 50 mg tablets
- Prednisone Oral Solution 5 mg per 5 mL
- Prednisone Intensol™ Oral Solution (Concentrate) 5 mg per mL
- Prednisone delayed-release tablets (Rayos) 1 mg, 2 mg, and 5 mg

- live vaccines, which should usually be avoided;
- cyclosporine, which interacts in both directions and raises the risk of seizures; and
- birth control pills and hormone therapy.
This list is not complete. Many other prescription medicines, over-the-counter products, vitamins and herbal products can interact with prednisone. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

- Avoid being near people who are sick or have an infection. Call your doctor if you are exposed to chickenpox or measles.
- Do not have a live vaccine, such as MMR, chickenpox, rotavirus, yellow fever, oral typhoid, or the nasal flu vaccine, without your doctor's approval. Avoid close contact with someone who has just had an oral or nasal live vaccine.
- Limit alcohol. Both alcohol and prednisone irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach bleeding.
- Be careful with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin, since taking them with prednisone raises the risk of stomach bleeding.
- Your doctor may ask you to cut back on salt, since prednisone makes your body hold onto fluid.

Generic versions are also manufactured by several other companies.
Ezallor Sprinkle (rosuvastatin) has been discontinued and is no longer available.

- Dose range: 5 mg to 40 mg once daily. The dose depends on the reason you are taking it, your LDL cholesterol level, and your individual risk of cardiovascular events.

- Severe kidney impairment (not on hemodialysis): the recommended starting dose is 5 mg once daily, and the dose should not exceed 10 mg once daily.
- Children with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia: 20 mg once daily for those 7 years of age and older.

- Take rosuvastatin exactly as your doctor tells you to.
- Take rosuvastatin by mouth once daily. Swallow the tablet whole.
- Rosuvastatin can be taken at any time of day, with or without food.
- Do not change your dose or stop this medicine without talking to your doctor, even if you are feeling well.
- Your doctor may do blood tests to check your cholesterol levels before and during your treatment with rosuvastatin. Your doctor may change your dose if needed.

- If you take an antacid that contains a combination of aluminum and magnesium hydroxide, take rosuvastatin at least 2 hours before you take the antacid.

Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant, or are planning to become pregnant. Rosuvastatin may harm your unborn baby. If you become pregnant while taking rosuvastatin, call your doctor right away to discuss your treatment.
Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. Medicines like rosuvastatin can pass into your breast milk and may harm your baby. Talk to your doctor about the best way to feed your baby if you take this medicine. Do not breastfeed while taking rosuvastatin.

- Store rosuvastatin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C).
- Store in a dry place.
- Safely throw away medicine that is out of date or no longer needed.
- Keep this and all medicines out of the reach of children.

Generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets may contain different inactive ingredients from those listed above. Check the product label for your particular formulation for a complete list of ingredients.

Common side effects:
The most common side effects may include headache, nausea, muscle aches and pains, weakness, and constipation.
Serious side effects:
Rosuvastatin may cause serious side effects, including:
- Muscle pain, tenderness and weakness (myopathy). Muscle problems, including muscle breakdown, can be serious in some people and rarely cause kidney damage that can lead to death. Tell your doctor right away if: you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you have a fever or feel more tired than usual, while you take this medicine. you have muscle problems that do not go away even after your doctor has told you to stop taking this medicine. Your doctor may do further tests to diagnose the cause of your muscle problems. Your chances of getting muscle problems are higher if you: are taking certain other medicines while you take rosuvastatin are 65 years of age or older are of Asian descent have thyroid problems (hypothyroidism) that are not controlled have kidney problems are taking higher doses of this medicine

- Liver problems. Your doctor may do blood tests to check your liver before you start taking this medicine and if you have symptoms of liver problems while you are taking it.
