Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:

- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.
Sertraline side effects in children and teenagers:
The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.
Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.
Other reported side effects:

Less common side effects reported during studies include tachycardia (fast heartbeat), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), underactive thyroid, enlarged pupils, blurred vision, blood in the stools, swelling, unsteady walking, irritability, fever, raised liver enzymes, anaphylaxis, diabetes, high cholesterol, low blood sugar, increased appetite, joint pain, muscle spasms, poor coordination, coma, convulsions, reduced alertness, numbness, lethargy, restlessness, fainting, aggression, teeth grinding, confusion, euphoric mood, hallucination, blood in the urine, milk production from the breasts, priapism (a long-lasting erection), vaginal bleeding, wheezing, yawning, hair loss, cold sweats, skin inflammation, blistering, itching, rash, hives, bleeding, high blood pressure, and flushing.

Side effects reported after sertraline came onto the market include increased clotting times, AV block, slow heartbeat, atrial arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia including Torsade de Pointes, breast enlargement in men, raised prolactin, irregular periods, SIADH, blindness, optic neuritis, cataract, severe liver problems including hepatitis, jaundice, and liver failure with some fatal outcomes, pancreatitis, several blood disorders, angioedema, low sodium, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), lockjaw, serotonin syndrome, movement disorders including akathisia and dystonia, psychosis, bedwetting, nightmares, sudden kidney failure, pulmonary hypertension, eosinophilic pneumonia, loss of smell, photosensitivity, severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, spasm of blood vessels in the brain, and vasculitis.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take sertraline with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), or within 14 days of stopping one, because of the risk of serotonin syndrome. This includes the antibiotic linezolid and intravenous methylene blue. You also need to wait at least 14 days after stopping sertraline before starting an MAOI.
Do not take sertraline with pimozide, an antipsychotic medicine. Do not take sertraline oral solution if you take disulfiram (Antabuse), because the solution contains alcohol.
Sertraline can raise the risk of bleeding, particularly if you also take aspirin, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, other antiplatelet medicines, warfarin, or other anticoagulants.
Screening for a personal or family history of bipolar disorder, mania, or hypomania is recommended before starting sertraline, since treating a depressive episode with an antidepressant can trigger a manic episode in someone with bipolar disorder.
Do not stop taking sertraline suddenly. Adverse reactions can occur when it is stopped, especially when it is stopped abruptly, so the dose should be lowered gradually where possible.
Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the one you missed and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Effects reported after a sertraline tablet overdose include seizures, which may be delayed, and changes in mental state including coma. Heart effects can also be delayed and include changes in the electrical activity of the heart (QRS and QTc prolongation). High blood pressure is seen most often, and low blood pressure is rare, though it can happen when other substances including alcohol have also been taken. Serotonin syndrome can occur, and the risk is higher when several drugs that raise serotonin have been taken together.

Sertraline is a prescription medicine used to treat depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). It is sold under the brand name Zoloft, and generic sertraline is widely available.
Sertraline belongs to a group of medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. It increases serotonin activity in the brain by blocking the reuptake of serotonin (a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to communicate) back into nerve cells, so more of it stays available. Sertraline has only very weak effects on the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, and it does not block monoamine oxidase.
Sertraline is available as tablets (25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL), and capsules (150 mg and 200 mg).
Sertraline is not a controlled substance.

Sertraline is FDA-approved to treat six conditions in adults:
- Major depressive disorder (MDD), the clinical term for depression.
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), where unwanted thoughts drive repeated behaviors.
- Panic disorder, which causes sudden attacks of intense fear along with physical symptoms.
- Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which can follow a frightening or traumatic event.
- Social anxiety disorder (SAD), also called social phobia.
- Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a severe form of premenstrual symptoms.
In children and teenagers, sertraline is approved only for OCD, from age 6 upward. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children under 6 years of age, or in children and teenagers for any condition other than OCD.
Not every sertraline product is approved for all six conditions:
- Sertraline tablets and oral solution are approved for all of them.
- Sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules are approved only for depression in adults and for OCD in adults and children aged 6 and over.

The usual starting dose of sertraline is 25 mg or 50 mg once a day, depending on the condition being treated, and the usual treatment range is 50 mg to 200 mg a day. The maximum dose for most conditions is 200 mg a day.
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range or maximum
Depression (MDD), adults | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, adults | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, ages 6 to 12 | 25 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, ages 13 to 17 | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
Panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder | 25 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
PMDD, taken every day | 50 mg a day | Up to 150 mg a day
PMDD, taken in the luteal phase only | 50 mg a day | Up to 100 mg a day
If the starting dose is not enough, the dose can be raised in steps of 25 mg to 50 mg a day. Because sertraline stays in the body for about 24 hours, doses are usually changed no more often than once a week.

Dosing for PMDD. Sertraline can be taken every day of the menstrual cycle, or only during the luteal phase, meaning you start 14 days before your period is due and continue until it starts, then repeat with each cycle. On daily dosing, the dose can go up by 50 mg per cycle to a maximum of 150 mg a day. On luteal phase dosing, the maximum is 100 mg a day, taken as 50 mg for the first 3 days of the dosing cycle and 100 mg for the rest of it.
Sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules. These are not used to start treatment or to titrate a dose, because there are no lower capsule strengths. They can be started in someone who has been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week. The recommended capsule dose is 150 mg or 200 mg once a day, and the maximum is 200 mg a day. Because the dose cannot be lowered in steps using capsules alone, coming off treatment requires switching back to another sertraline product.

Liver problems. With sertraline tablets and oral solution, mild liver impairment (Child-Pugh score 5 or 6) means both the starting dose and the usual range are halved, and use is not recommended in moderate or severe liver impairment (Child-Pugh score 7 to 15). Sertraline capsules are not recommended in mild, moderate, or severe liver impairment, because the dose cannot be adjusted with the strengths available.
Kidney problems. No dose change is needed for mild, moderate, or severe kidney impairment, including in people on dialysis.

Several medicines interact with sertraline. Give a full list of everything you take to any provider who treats you. The most important interactions are:
- MAOIs. Taking sertraline with an MAOI raises the risk of serotonin syndrome, and the combination is contraindicated. Examples include selegiline, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, phenelzine, linezolid, and methylene blue.
- Pimozide. Sertraline raises pimozide levels, which can lead to QTc prolongation and irregular heartbeats. The combination is contraindicated.
- Other medicines that raise serotonin. These add to the risk of serotonin syndrome. Examples include other SSRIs and SNRIs, triptans for migraine, tricyclic antidepressants, opioids, lithium, tryptophan, buspirone, amphetamines, and St. John's wort.
- Blood thinners and antiplatelet medicines. Aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin, and warfarin can add to the bleeding risk. If you take warfarin, your INR should be monitored carefully.

- Medicines broken down by CYP2D6. Sertraline blocks this liver enzyme, so levels of these drugs can rise and doses may need to be lowered. Examples include propafenone, flecainide, atomoxetine, desipramine, dextromethorphan, metoprolol, nebivolol, perphenazine, thioridazine, tolterodine, and venlafaxine.
- Phenytoin and fosphenytoin. Sertraline can raise phenytoin levels, so levels should be checked when sertraline is started or the dose is changed.
- Medicines that prolong the QTc interval. These should generally be avoided. Examples include certain antipsychotics (ziprasidone, iloperidone, chlorpromazine, mesoridazine, droperidol), certain antibiotics (erythromycin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin, sparfloxacin), Class 1A antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide), Class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol), and others including pentamidine, methadone, halofantrine, mefloquine, dolasetron, probucol, and tacrolimus.
- Disulfiram, with the oral solution only, because of its alcohol content.

No dose adjustment is needed when sertraline is taken with cimetidine, diazepam, lithium, atenolol, tolbutamide, digoxin, or medicines broken down by CYP3A4.
This list is not complete. Many other prescription medicines, over-the-counter products, vitamins, and herbal products can interact with sertraline.

- Do not drink alcohol while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not add to the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but drinking is still not recommended during treatment.
- Do not drive or operate machinery until you know how sertraline affects you. It can cause sleepiness and can affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly.
- Do not start or stop any other medicine without checking first, including over-the-counter products, vitamins, and herbal supplements.

- a thyroid disorder; or
- if you drink more than 2 alcoholic beverages daily
- a muscle weakness condition (such as myasthenia gravis or ocular myasthenia).
Simvastatin can cause a condition that results in the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue, potentially leading to kidney failure. This condition may be more likely to occur in older adults and in people who have kidney disease or poorly controlled hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid).
This medicine can harm an unborn baby or cause birth defects. Do not take simvastatin if you are pregnant. Stop taking this medication and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Use effective birth control to avoid pregnancy while you are taking this medicine.
Simvastatin may pass into breast milk and could harm a nursing baby. Do not breast-feed while you are taking this medicine.

Take simvastatin exactly as prescribed. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Never take this medicine in larger amounts, or for longer than prescribed. Taking too much of this medication may cause serious or life-threatening side effects.
Simvastatin is usually taken once a day in the evening. If you are taking the oral suspension, take it on an empty stomach. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose to make sure you get the best results.
If you are taking the oral suspension, shake the bottle well for at least 20 seconds before each use. Measure the medicine with an accurate measuring device, not a regular household spoon.
While using simvastatin, you may need frequent blood tests at your doctor's office.
You may need to take simvastatin on a long-term basis for the treatment of high cholesterol. You may need to stop using this medicine for a short time if you have surgery or a medical emergency. Do not stop taking this medicine unless your doctor tells you to.

Simvastatin is only part of a complete program of treatment that also includes diet, exercise, and weight control. Follow your diet, medication, and exercise routines very closely.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to simvastatin (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Simvastatin can cause the breakdown of muscle tissue, which can lead to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, or dark urine.
Also call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of a kidney problem - little or no urinating; painful or difficult urination; swelling in your feet or ankles; feeling tired or short of breath; or
- muscle weakness in your hips, shoulders, neck, and back;
- trouble lifting your arms, trouble climbing or standing; or
- liver problems - nausea, upper stomach pain, itching, tired feeling, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes).
Common simvastatin side effects may include:
- headache;
- constipation, nausea, stomach pain; or

- cold symptoms such as stuffy nose, sneezing, sore throat.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

In rare cases, simvastatin can cause a condition that results in the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue, potentially leading to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, and dark colored urine.
Never take simvastatin in larger amounts, or for longer than recommended by your doctor. Follow your doctor's dosing instructions very carefully. Taking too much of this medication may cause serious or life-threatening side effects.
Before taking this medicine, tell your doctor if you have ever had liver or kidney disease, diabetes, a thyroid disorder, a muscle weakness condition (such as myasthenia gravis or ocular myasthenia), if you are of Chinese descent, or if you drink more than 2 alcoholic beverages daily.
Simvastatin can harm an unborn baby or cause birth defects. Do not use if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

Grapefruit and grapefruit juice may interact with simvastatin and lead to potentially dangerous effects. Do not consume grapefruit products while taking this medication.
Some medicines can cause unwanted or dangerous effects when used with simvastatin. Your doctor may need to change your treatment plan if you use certain antibiotics or antifungal medicines, heart medication, antiviral medications such as hepatitis C medications, HIV/AIDS medications, or Paxlovid for COVID-19.
Stop taking this medication and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant.
Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. Skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. Do not take extra medicine to make up the missed dose.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.

Simvastatin belongs to a group of drugs called HMG CoA reductase inhibitors, or "statins."
Simvastatin is used to lower blood levels of "bad" cholesterol (low-density lipoprotein, or LDL), to increase levels of "good" cholesterol (high-density lipoprotein, or HDL), and to lower triglycerides (a type of fat in the blood).
Simvastatin is also used to lower the risk of stroke, heart attack, and other heart complications in people with diabetes, coronary heart disease, or other risk factors.
Simvastatin is used in adults and children who are at least 10 years old.

Many drugs can interact with simvastatin. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your medications and any you start or stop using during treatment, especially:
- delavirdine;
- fenofibrate; or
- fluconazole.
Your doctor may need to change your treatment plan if you use certain antibiotics or antifungal medicines, heart medication, antiviral medications such as hepatitis C medications, HIV/AIDS medications, or Paxlovid for COVID-19. This list is not complete and many other drugs can interact with simvastatin. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

Grapefruit and grapefruit juice may interact with simvastatin and lead to unwanted side effects. Avoid the use of grapefruit products while taking this medicine.
Avoid eating foods that are high in fat or cholesterol. Simvastatin will not be as effective in lowering your cholesterol if you do not follow a cholesterol-lowering diet plan.
Avoid drinking alcohol. It can raise triglyceride levels and may increase your risk of liver damage.

Spironolactone blocks the effect of male hormones, and male hormones are needed for a male baby to develop normally. In animal studies, male offspring exposed in the womb showed feminized development. The limited information available in humans has not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern remains. Your doctor will usually avoid spironolactone in pregnancy, or talk through the possible risk to a male baby with you. Untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry real risks in pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than by stopping on your own.
Breastfeeding:
Spironolactone itself does not pass into breast milk. Its active breakdown product, canrenone, has been found in breast milk in very small amounts that are not expected to affect a breastfed baby. No side effects were reported in the one infant studied over a short period, and the long-term picture is not known. Talk to your doctor so you can weigh this up together.
Children:

Spironolactone has not been shown to be safe and effective in children. The oral liquid is specifically not recommended for treating high blood pressure in children, because of the hormonal effects of the medicine. Any use in a child must be decided and monitored by a specialist.
Older adults:
Spironolactone is cleared by the kidneys, and kidney function tends to fall with age. Older adults are therefore more likely to build up a high potassium level, so kidney function and potassium need monitoring.

Take spironolactone exactly as prescribed. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides.
- Take it the same way each day, either always with food or always without. Food increases how much spironolactone your body absorbs, roughly doubling it, so switching back and forth changes how much medicine you actually get.
- Shake the oral liquid well before every dose, and measure it with the marked oral syringe, dosing spoon, or medicine cup that comes with it, not a kitchen spoon.
- Do not switch between tablets and the oral liquid without your doctor changing the dose. They are not interchangeable, and the liquid gives a higher level of medicine in your blood for the same number of milligrams.
- You will need regular blood tests to check your potassium, sodium, kidney function, uric acid, and blood sugar. Keep these appointments even if you feel completely well.
- If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep taking spironolactone even when you feel fine. High blood pressure usually has no symptoms.

- Tell any doctor or dentist treating you that you take spironolactone, and tell your surgeon before any operation.
- Spironolactone can interfere with one type of blood test used to measure digoxin, so mention it if you take digoxin.
- Do not share this medicine with anyone else.
- Store tablets at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C), and protect them from light. Store the oral liquid at room temperature and keep it in a tightly closed bottle.

Is spironolactone a diuretic?:
Yes. Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and it belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics. It works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water. Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in. It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason it is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one.
Is spironolactone used for acne?:
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label for hormonal acne in women. Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but it means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose.

The reason it is used this way relates to how spironolactone works. As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone. Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne.
Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it. Any dose is chosen by the prescriber. Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because it may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking it for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.
If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever it is prescribed for.
Does spironolactone cause weight gain?:

Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and it is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information. Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid.
If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame. Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look. Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine.
Does spironolactone cause hair loss?:
Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often it happens is not known. It is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.

The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning. Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss. If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out.
How long does it take for spironolactone to work?:
It depends what you are taking it for. Spironolactone reaches its highest level in your blood in about 2 to 3 hours, and its active breakdown product peaks at around 4 hours, so it starts having an effect on your kidneys the same day.

The results you notice take longer. For fluid build-up, spironolactone is given for at least five days before the dose is increased, because that is how long the full effect takes to show. For high blood pressure, the dose is adjusted at two-week intervals, so give it a couple of weeks before judging it. For heart failure, the benefit is a lower risk of being admitted to hospital and living longer, which is not something you feel week to week.
How long does spironolactone stay in your system?:
Spironolactone itself leaves your blood very quickly, with a half-life of about 1.4 hours, meaning half of it is gone in that time. Its active breakdown products last much longer, with half-lives of roughly 14 to 17 hours. Because of those, the effect of a dose carries on well after the spironolactone itself has gone, and it takes a few days for the medicine to clear fully after you stop. Clearance is slower if you have cirrhosis.
Is spironolactone a blood thinner?:

No. Spironolactone is not a blood thinner. It does not affect blood clotting and it is not used to prevent clots or strokes in the way that warfarin, apixaban, or aspirin are. It is a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid build-up.
Spironolactone does interact with some blood thinners indirectly. Heparin and low molecular weight heparin can raise potassium, so taking them with spironolactone increases the risk of a high potassium level.
Can I stop taking spironolactone suddenly?:
Spironolactone does not cause withdrawal symptoms and does not need to be tapered the way a steroid does. Even so, do not stop it without speaking to your doctor. Stopping it can allow fluid to build up again, your blood pressure to rise, or your heart failure to worsen, and if you are taking it for heart failure it is one of the medicines shown to help people live longer. If side effects are the reason you want to stop, a dose change or a different medicine may be an option.
Can you take spironolactone at night?:

There is no fixed time of day for spironolactone. What matters more is that you take it at the same time each day and always the same way with regard to food, since food changes how much you absorb. Many people prefer the morning because spironolactone makes you pass more urine, and a late dose can mean getting up in the night. If a nighttime dose suits you better, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you drink alcohol while taking spironolactone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and spironolactone, but drinking is best kept modest. Both can lower your blood pressure and make you light-headed, so together they raise the chance of feeling dizzy or faint, particularly when you stand up. Alcohol is also a problem in its own right if you are taking spironolactone for liver disease. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for your situation.
Can you take spironolactone while pregnant?:

Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy. It blocks the action of male hormones, and in animal studies male offspring exposed before birth developed abnormally. Human data are limited and have not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern is enough that the manufacturer advises avoiding it or discussing the potential risk to a male baby.
Do not stop spironolactone on your own if you find out you are pregnant. Tell your doctor straight away, because untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry serious risks in pregnancy and your treatment will need to be changed carefully.
Does spironolactone cause constipation?:
Constipation is not a listed side effect of spironolactone. The digestive side effects that have been reported are the opposite, including diarrhea and stomach cramping, along with nausea, vomiting, and indigestion. If you are constipated while taking spironolactone, another cause is more likely, and it is worth mentioning to your pharmacist, who can check the rest of your medicines.
Is 200 mg of spironolactone too much?:

It depends on the reason you are taking it. For fluid build-up, the approved dose range goes up to 200 mg a day, and for primary hyperaldosteronism it goes up to 400 mg a day, so 200 mg is within the licensed range for both.
For high blood pressure it would be above the usual range, since doses over 100 mg a day do not lower blood pressure any further. For heart failure the usual dose is 25 mg to 50 mg a day, so 200 mg would be well above what is normally used. Higher doses also carry a greater risk of high potassium and of breast growth in men. If your dose seems high for your condition, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting it yourself.
Why is spironolactone described as a high-risk medicine?:
The main reason is the risk of a high potassium level, which can cause a dangerous change in your heart rhythm and often gives no warning symptoms. The risk rises if your kidneys do not work well or if you take other medicines that raise potassium, and several very common medicines do, including ibuprofen and some blood pressure tablets.

This risk is manageable, which is why blood tests are built into treatment. Your potassium should be checked within a week of starting spironolactone or changing your dose, and regularly after that. Spironolactone also needs care in pregnancy and in people with liver disease.

Reported spironolactone side effects:
Reported spironolactone side effects include breast and nipple pain in both men and women, a lower sex drive, trouble getting or keeping an erection, irregular or missed periods, bleeding after menopause, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, feeling sluggish, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, indigestion, hair thinning, and itching.
The most common side effect of spironolactone is breast growth in men, known as gynecomastia. In the main heart failure study, about 9 in 100 men taking an average of 26 mg a day developed it. The chance goes up on higher doses. It can start anywhere from one or two months into treatment to more than a year later, and it usually goes away after the medicine is stopped.
Several of these effects are dose-related, so they are more likely on higher doses, and many settle after the dose is lowered or the medicine is stopped. How often most of them happen is not known, because they come from reports gathered after the medicine was approved rather than from counted numbers in trials.

- a skin rash that spreads or blisters, peeling skin, sores in your mouth, or a rash with a fever and swollen glands, which can be signs of a rare but serious skin reaction;
- yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pain in your upper stomach, which can be signs of a liver problem;
- a fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising or bleeding, which can be signs of a problem with your blood cells; or
- new confusion, unsteadiness, or extreme drowsiness if you have liver disease, since spironolactone can make brain function worse in people with cirrhosis.
Spironolactone side effects in men:
Men are most likely to notice effects linked to spironolactone blocking male hormones. These include breast growth and breast tenderness, a lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. Breast growth is dose related, so tell your doctor early rather than waiting, since a lower dose or a different medicine may be an option.
Spironolactone side effects in women:

Women may notice irregular periods, missed periods, breast tenderness, or bleeding after menopause. Some women also notice patchy darkening of the skin on the face. Report any unexpected bleeding after menopause to your doctor so it can be checked properly rather than assumed to be a side effect.
Long-term spironolactone side effects:
The main long-term concerns with spironolactone are chemical rather than something you would feel. Over time it can push your potassium too high, and it can also lower your sodium, magnesium, and calcium, raise your blood sugar, and raise your uric acid, which occasionally brings on gout. This is why you need regular blood tests for as long as you take it, not just at the start.
In animal studies, spironolactone given at high doses over long periods caused tumors in rats, mainly in hormone-producing glands and the liver. No increase in tumors was seen at the lower doses tested, which were still around five times the highest recommended human dose when adjusted for body size. Whether this happens in people is not known.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take spironolactone if you have a high potassium level in your blood, if you have Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder), or if you are taking eplerenone (Inspra), another medicine of the same type.
Spironolactone can raise your potassium to a dangerous level. A high potassium level can cause a life-threatening change in your heart rhythm, and it often causes no symptoms until it is already high. Your doctor should check your potassium with a blood test within a week of you starting spironolactone or having your dose changed, and regularly after that.
Your risk of high potassium is greater if your kidneys do not work well, if you take potassium supplements or a salt substitute containing potassium, or if you take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, an NSAID, heparin, or trimethoprim.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor has specifically told you to.

Passing too much fluid can drop your blood pressure and make your kidney function worse, especially if you are also taking an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Tell your doctor if you feel faint, or if you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhea.
If you have cirrhosis with fluid in your abdomen, spironolactone is usually started in hospital, because sudden shifts in fluid and salt can affect how your brain works.
Spironolactone should be avoided in pregnancy where possible, because it blocks male hormones and may affect how a male baby develops.
Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. Skip it if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Taking too much spironolactone can cause drowsiness, confusion, a rash, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or diarrhea. A dangerously high potassium level is the main serious risk, particularly if your kidneys do not work well.

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) used for heart failure, high blood pressure, fluid build-up (edema) caused by liver or kidney disease, and a hormone condition called primary hyperaldosteronism. Spironolactone is sometimes prescribed off-label for women with acne or excessive facial hair growth (hirsutism).
Spironolactone works by blocking a hormone called aldosterone, which causes your body to pass more salt and water in your urine while keeping potassium in. This is why it is called potassium-sparing, and it is what makes spironolactone different from most other water pills, which flush potassium out.
Spironolactone also blocks androgens such as testosterone from binding to the androgen receptor, which explains several of its side effects, including breast tenderness and breast growth.
Spironolactone is FDA-approved to treat adults with:

- Heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV) with a reduced ejection fraction to help live longer, reduce swelling, and reduce the need for hospital stays. It is taken alongside other heart failure medicines rather than on its own.
- High blood pressure as an add-on treatment for people whose blood pressure is not controlled well enough by other medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of stroke and heart attack.
- Fluid build-up (edema) caused by cirrhosis of the liver when cutting back on fluid and salt has not been enough, and also for swelling caused by nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder) when treating the underlying disease and using other water pills have not worked well enough.
- Primary hyperaldosteronism, which is a condition where the adrenal glands make too much aldosterone. Spironolactone is used short-term to prepare for surgery, and long-term for people who are not suitable for surgery.

Spironolactone tablets come in 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg strengths. Spironolactone 25 mg is the strength most often used to start treatment. There is also a banana-flavored oral liquid for people who cannot swallow tablets. The liquid and the tablets are not interchangeable, so never switch between them without your doctor changing your dose.

The usual starting dose of spironolactone tablets for adults is 25 mg to 100 mg a day, depending on the condition being treated. Your doctor will pick a starting dose and then adjust it based on your blood tests and how you respond.
Spironolactone dosage for heart failure:
Treatment starts at spironolactone 25 mg once a day, provided your potassium level is 5.0 mEq/L or lower and your kidney function (eGFR) is above 50. If you tolerate that, the dose may go up to 50 mg once a day. If your potassium rises too high, the dose may drop to 25 mg every other day. If your eGFR is between 30 and 50, your doctor may start you at 25 mg every other day because of the higher risk of high potassium.
Spironolactone dosage for high blood pressure:
The usual starting dose is spironolactone 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as one dose or split into two. The dose can be adjusted every two weeks. Doses above 100 mg a day do not generally lower blood pressure any further.
Spironolactone dosage for fluid build-up (edema):

The usual starting dose is 100 mg a day, taken as one dose or split into two, and the dose can range from 25 mg to 200 mg a day. If you have cirrhosis, treatment is started in hospital and increased slowly. When spironolactone is the only water pill being used, it is given for at least five days before the dose is increased.
Spironolactone dosage for primary hyperaldosteronism:
The dose is 100 mg to 400 mg a day when preparing for surger y. For people who are not suitable for surgery, the lowest dose that works is used long term.
Spironolactone oral liquid doses:
The oral liquid has its own separate doses because it is absorbed differently. Heart failure starts at 20 mg (4 mL) once a day. High blood pressure starts at 20 mg (4 mL) to 75 mg (15 mL) a day. Swelling from cirrhosis starts at 75 mg (15 mL) a day, begun in hospital. If more than 100 mg a day is needed, a different form of the medicine should be used instead.
Spironolactone formulations:
- Spironolactone 25 mg tablets
- Spironolactone 50 mg tablets
- Spironolactone 100 mg tablets
- Spironolactone oral suspension 25 mg per 5 mL

- Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes containing potassium, and low-sodium products that use potassium instead of salt. Check labels, since potassium chloride is a common salt replacement.
- Go easy on foods very high in potassium if your doctor has told you to. This is worth asking about specifically, because most people are told to eat more potassium, not less.
- Be careful with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen. They can push your potassium up, make spironolactone work less well, and strain your kidneys.
- Limit alcohol. It can add to the dizziness and light-headedness, especially when you first start.
- Avoid getting up quickly from sitting or lying down, and avoid driving or anything hazardous until you know how spironolactone affects you.
- Do not take another medicine containing spironolactone at the same time, such as Aldactazide, and do not take eplerenone.

To make sure tamsulosin is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- an allergy to tamsulosin or any of its ingredients
- an allergy to sulfa drugs
- kidney problems
- liver problems
- low blood pressure (hypotension)
Also tell your doctor if you are planning to have cataract or glaucoma surgery.
Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before starting tamsulosin and at regular intervals afterwards.
Tamsulosin is not approved for use in women or in children.

Take tamsulosin exactly as prescribed. Follow the directions on your prescription label and read any medication guides or instruction sheets.
- Take once a day, about 30 minutes after the same meal each day. For example, 30 minutes after dinner.
- Swallow the capsule whole. Do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
- If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, do not start again without talking to your doctor.
- Store at room temperature, away from moisture and heat.
Dosing information:
Usual adult dose for benign prostatic hyperplasia:
- 0.4 mg by mouth once a day, taken about half an hour after the same meal each day.
- If symptoms have not improved after 2 to 4 weeks at 0.4 mg, the dose may be increased to 0.8 mg once a day.
- Tamsulosin 0.4 mg should not be taken with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole.
- If tamsulosin is stopped or interrupted for several days, treatment should start again at 0.4 mg once a day.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, itching, rash, swelling of your face, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing. Rarely, tamsulosin has been linked to severe skin reactions with blistering and peeling of the skin.
Stop taking tamsulosin and call your doctor at once if you have:
- a lightheaded feeling, like you might pass out
- a painful erection that will not go away and is not related to sexual activity
What are the common side effects of tamsulosin?:
Common tamsulosin side effects may include:
- headache
- dizziness
- runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, cough, sinus congestion
- flu-like symptoms or infection
- weakness or lack of energy
- back pain, chest pain
- diarrhea, nausea
- drowsiness or trouble sleeping
- tooth problems
- abnormal ejaculation, including a smaller amount of semen or no semen at all
- reduced interest in sex
- blurred vision

Some side effects are more likely at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at the usual 0.4 mg starting dose. In clinical studies, abnormal ejaculation was reported by about 8 in 100 men taking 0.4 mg and about 18 in 100 men taking 0.8 mg. Blurred vision was reported by about 2 in 100 men taking 0.8 mg, and was uncommon at 0.4 mg.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.

An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If you have missed the dose for the whole day, skip it and take your next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days in a row, talk to your doctor before starting again.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose can cause a serious drop in blood pressure. Lying down flat can help until medical help arrives.

Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH. These symptoms include a weak urine stream, trouble starting to urinate, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely, needing to urinate often or urgently, and getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers. It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck. Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there, which improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax, which has now been discontinued in the U.S., but generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure, and it is not approved for use in women or children.

Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood and increase the risk of side effects.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
- strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
- other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
- moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
- strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
- cimetidine
- warfarin
- medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra). Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg. Your doctor will decide what is right for you.

No dose change is needed if you take tamsulosin with nifedipine, atenolol, enalapril, digoxin, theophylline, or furosemide.
This list is not complete, and many other medicines may interact with tamsulosin. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

Single-dose pens and vials (Zepbound and Mounjaro)
- Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C).
- Do not freeze. Do not use if the medication has been frozen.
- Keep in the original carton until use to protect from light.
- If needed, single-dose pens and vials may be kept at room temperature up to 86°F (30°C) for up to 21 days. Once at room temperature, do not return to the refrigerator.
- Discard after 21 days at room temperature if unused.
KwikPen (Zepbound KwikPen and Mounjaro KwikPen)
Before first use:
- Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C).
- Keep until the expiration date printed on the label.
- Do not freeze. Discard the pen if it has been frozen.
After first use:

- Store in the refrigerator or at room temperature up to 86°F (30°C).
- Keep away from heat and light.
- Discard the pen 30 days after first use, even if medicine remains.
- Discard after 4 weekly doses have been given.
General storage advice (all tirzepatide products)
- Keep all pens, vials, needles, and syringes out of reach of children.
- Dispose of used pens, needles, and syringes in an approved sharps container.

Usual Zepbound Dose for Weight Loss and OSA (Adult):
- Initial dose: 2.5 mg under the skin (subcutaneously) once a week.
- After 4 weeks: The dosage should be increased to 5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- Further dose increases: After at least 4 weeks on the current dose, the dosage may be increased in 2.5 mg increments.
- Recommended maintenance dose for weight loss: 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
- Recommended maintenance dose for OSA: 10 mg or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
- Maximum dose: 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Dose of Mounjaro for Type 2 Diabetes (Adults and Children 10 Years and Older):
- Initial dose: 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- If additional glycemic control is needed: Increase the dose in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
- Maximum dose (adults): 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- Maximum dose (children 10 years and older): 10 mg subcutaneously once a week.
- Comments: The starting dose and escalation schedule are designed to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal side effects.

Dose of Mounjaro to Reduce Cardiovascular Risk (Adults With Type 2 Diabetes at High Risk):
- The same dosing and escalation schedule applies.
- Start at 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week and increase in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose, up to a maximum of 15 mg once a week.
- In the SURPASS-CVOT trial, participants were titrated to 15 mg once weekly or their maximum tolerated dose.
How to Use Mounjaro:
- Give once weekly at any time of day, with or without meals.
- Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen or thigh. Another person may inject into the back of the upper arm. Rotate injection sites with each dose.
- Missed dose: Give as soon as possible within 4 days (96 hours). If more than 4 days have passed, skip the missed dose and give the next dose on the regularly scheduled day.
- The day of weekly administration can be changed, if necessary, as long as the time between the 2 doses is at least 3 days (72 hours).

You should follow the directions on your prescription label carefully and ask your pharmacist or doctor to explain any part you do not understand. It is important to use this medicine exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed by your doctor.
Tirzepatide is injected under the skin (subcutaneously) using a pre-filled single-dose pen, a multi-dose KwikPen (for single patient use), and a single-dose vial with a syringe. Caregivers or patients should be trained on proper injection techniques and should read the instructions for use. Children should not inject themselves with the KwikPen; an adult caregiver should give a child their injections.
Tirzepatide is usually given:
- once a week.
- can be given with or without meals at any time of the day.
- may be injected into the thigh, abdomen, or have another person inject it into the back of your upper arm
- You should rotate injection sites with each dose.
- Do not inject into a muscle (intramuscularly) or vein (intravenously).

- Do not mix insulin and tirzepatide together in the same injection. You may give an injection of tirzepatide and insulin in the same body area, but not right next to each other.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose, which may be gradually increased, but not more than once every 4 weeks.
You may change the day of the week you use tirzepatide as long as there are at least three days between doses.
Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor.
Tirzepatide KwikPen:
The KwikPen contains 4 fixed doses, and one dose is injected weekly (subcutaneously).
- For your weekly dose, you need to turn the dose knob all the way until it stops AND the 1 icon is in the dose window.
- After 4 doses, throw away (discard) the Pen, including the unused medicine. The Pen will prevent you from dialing a full dose after you have given yourself 4 weekly doses. Do not inject the leftover medicine. Do not transfer the leftover medicine from your Pen into a syringe.

- Do not share your tirzepatide Pen with other people, even if the pen needle has been changed. You may give other people a serious infection or get a serious infection from them.
- People who are blind or have vision problems should not use the Pen without help from a person who has been trained to use the pen.

Who should not use tirzepatide:
- Type 1 diabetes patients (tirzepatide is not approved for type 1 diabetes)
- Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)
- Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Use with Caution:
- History of pancreatitis (safety not established in patients with prior pancreatitis)
- Severe gastrointestinal disease
- Diabetic retinopathy complications.

Tell your doctor and pharmacist what prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are planning to take or are taking. They may interact with tirzepatide, and your doctor may need to change the doses of your medications or monitor you carefully for side effects.
Birth control pills may not work as well while receiving this medicine. Your doctor may suggest you use another form of birth control for 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide and for 4 weeks after each dose change.
Taking tirzepatide with other medicines to treat diabetes, such as sulfonylureas or insulin, may increase your risk of hypoglycemia. Talk to your doctor and pharmacist about low blood sugar and how to manage it.
This medicine delays gastric emptying and may alter the absorption of other orally administered medicines.

In the Mounjaro prescribing information, SURPASS-1 (NCT03954834) was a 40-week trial in adults with type 2 diabetes whose blood sugar was not adequately controlled with diet and exercise alone. Patients received once-weekly Mounjaro 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg, or placebo.
After 40 weeks, 78% to 85% of adults taking Mounjaro achieved an HbA1c below 7%, compared with 23% of adults taking a placebo.
The average HbA1c change was -1.8% with Mounjaro 5 mg, -1.7% with Mounjaro 10 mg, and -1.7% with Mounjaro 15 mg, compared with -0.1% with placebo.

SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease to Mounjaro (tirzepatide, up to 15 mg once weekly) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly, a GLP-1 medicine already approved to reduce cardiovascular risk, with a median follow-up of about 4 years.
- Cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke occurred in 12.1% of those taking Mounjaro compared with 13.0% of those taking dulaglutide (HR 0.92, 95.3% CI 0.83–1.01), meeting the trial's goal of non-inferiority but not demonstrating superiority.
- Death from any cause occurred in 8.5% of the Mounjaro group versus 10.1% of the dulaglutide group (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75–0.94), though this was not a primary endpoint and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it should be read as exploratory.
Because the comparator was an active medicine rather than placebo, these results describe how Mounjaro performs against another GLP-1, not how much it lowers risk compared with no treatment.

Common Side Effects:
The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Constipation
- Nausea (mild to moderate)
- Decreased appetite
- Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
- Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
- Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems. Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
- Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.

- Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
- Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
- Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
- Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
- Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation. Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Tirzepatide carries a Boxed Warning for the risk of possible thyroid tumors.
Possible Thyroid Tumors (Including Cancer):
Tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath. These may be symptoms of thyroid cancer. In studies with rats, tirzepatide and medicines that work like tirzepatide have caused thyroid tumors, including thyroid cancer. It is not known if tirzepatide will cause thyroid tumors, or a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in people.
Do not use tirzepatide if you or any of your family have ever had a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or if you have an endocrine system condition called Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

In case of overdose, call the poison control helpline at 1-800-222-1222. Information is also available online at Poison Help. If the victim has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing, or can't be awakened, immediately call emergency services at 911.

Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk).
Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition. Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise. It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.

Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

If you miss a dose of tirzepatide, take the missed dose as soon as you remember it, if within 4 days after the missed dose. However, if it has been more than 4 days since your last dose, then skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not inject two doses within 3 days of each other.
